stories.headline: Coalition to move away from fossil fuels presses ahead without Colombia, its original champion
stories.deck: The coalition, launched in the Colombian coastal city of Santa Marta in April, is expected to release a progress report this week outlining steps taken by participating countries, including additional national plans to reduce dependence on coal, oil and gas
stories.bodyText:
A coalition of countries seeking to accelerate the global transition away from fossil fuels is preparing to unveil new national plans at the ongoing United Nations climate talks, known as COP31, in Antalya, Turkey, pressing ahead despite the withdrawal of Colombia, one of its founding members.
The coalition, launched in the Colombian coastal city of Santa Marta in April, is expected to release a progress report this week outlining steps taken by participating countries, including additional national plans to reduce dependence on coal, oil and gas.
The announcement comes as Ireland and the Pacific island nation of Tuvalu prepare to take over leadership of the initiative from Colombia and the Netherlands, with a second international conference planned for July 2027.
A statement from Ireland's Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment confirmed Colombia's withdrawal and said preparations were well advanced for a program of events in both countries next year. Neither the Environment Ministry nor the presidential office responded to questions about Colombia's withdrawal or its plans to attend the next conference.
“This process is bigger than any one country,” the department said, adding that further details would be announced at a formal handover during COP31.
A coalition seeking to turn promises into action
The Santa Marta conference emerged from frustration over the slow pace of international efforts to reduce dependence on coal, oil and gas, the fossil fuels that are the main drivers of global warming.
The initiative brought representatives from 57 countries together to explore ways of turning international commitments to move away from fossil fuels, the main drivers of global warming, into concrete national policies. Unlike formal UN climate negotiations, the gathering was designed to encourage open discussions without pressure to reach binding agreements or commit to specific deadlines.
Colombia's withdrawal follows the election of President Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office in August promising to strengthen the country's oil and gas industry and revive exploration. He succeeded leftist President Gustavo Petro, who had made moving away from fossil fuels a central pillar of his environmental agenda and stopped awarding new oil and gas exploration contracts.
Colombia's Environment Minister Fabio Arjona said in the past week that the previous administration's restrictions on gas development had contributed to domestic shortages, forcing some industries to rely on more polluting fuels. He argued that expanding supplies of natural gas, itself a fossil fuel, would help reduce emissions by replacing dirtier alternatives while ensuring the country's energy security.
Irene Velez, Colombia's former Environment Minister and one of the initiative's leading advocates, said the coalition had developed momentum beyond the government that helped establish it.
"Santa Marta has a life of its own, beyond the change of government in Colombia," Ms. Velez said.
From international pledges to national road maps
The coalition's future is being discussed as governments at COP31 confront renewed disagreements over how to accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels.
At the 2023 UN climate summit in Dubai, known as COP28, nearly 200 countries agreed for the first time to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems. But the agreement established no binding timetable, leaving governments to determine how to fulfill the commitment. Since then, little has happened on the international level toward reducing greenhouse gases.
This year at COP31, an initial outline of a possible agreement includes proposals to recognize a global fossil fuel transition road map developed by Brazil's COP30 presidency in 2025 and establish a process for advancing its recommendations.
The voluntary road map, published on November 3 and formally presented at COP31 a week later, outlines ways countries can reduce their dependence on coal, oil and gas according to their economic circumstances.
Natalie Jones, a senior policy adviser at the International Institute for Sustainable Development, said 23 countries had announced national or regional road maps or plans to develop them and the Santa Marta coalition was advancing work on national road maps, trade, economic policies and financial incentives.
"Planning is the first step towards delivering the transition," Ms. Jones said.
Ms. Velez pointed to initiatives in Finland, Germany, Ireland and the Netherlands, alongside efforts by the United Kingdom and Brazil to develop their own road maps, as evidence of growing momentum.
But questions remain over whether voluntary commitments can produce meaningful reductions in fossil fuel production and consumption.
Joeri Rogelj, a professor of climate science and policy at Imperial College London, said progress since Santa Marta had been limited, with only a handful of countries publishing national transition road maps.
"The COP30 road map for transitioning away from fossil fuels is more a transitioning mood board than a map that one can use to navigate this transition," Rogelj said, suggesting it offers a broad vision rather than concrete steps countries can follow.
Still, he said the initiative could help countries identify different pathways away from fossil fuels, from replacing aging infrastructure with renewable energy to avoiding fossil fuel dependence altogether.
Ms. Jones said the global road map was a significant political step but warned that its voluntary nature meant governments would need to establish clear timelines and implement concrete policies.
COP31 puts fossil fuels back on the agenda
The debate is unfolding at COP31, where negotiators are considering whether to formally recognize the global road map and establish a process for carrying its recommendations into future climate negotiations.
Fanny Petitbon, a policy expert at environmental group 350.org, warned that dropping contested proposals in the face of opposition would undermine the summit's ambition.
"Cutting fossil fuel dependence and scaling up climate finance, including by making big polluters foot part of the bill, are two make-or-break issues for a successful COP outcome," she said.
Financing remains a major obstacle, particularly for developing countries dependent on fossil fuel revenues or lacking resources to expand renewable energy and supporting infrastructure.
Ms. Jones said vulnerable countries would need international support to diversify their economies and maintain public services as fossil fuel revenues decline.
The coalition also faces the challenge of attracting major fossil fuel producers, whose participation could determine whether it becomes a significant force in global energy policy.
Ms. Velez said she would not rule out greater involvement from major producers, suggesting China and some of its provincial governments could eventually become more interested as economic and energy security considerations increasingly influence the transition.
Organizers are preparing events in Ireland ahead of the expected 2027 conference in Tuvalu, where governments will face pressure to demonstrate progress beyond announcing new plans.
Ireland's government said it was committed to ensuring the next conference delivered "meaningful and lasting outcomes."

stories.headline: 'Handshake' deals could fall: Musk flags risks for Nvidia after Jensen Huang's exit
stories.deck: Elon Musk has voiced his apprehensions regarding Nvidia's supply chain deals in the wake of Jensen Huang's recent resignation. He pointed out that numerous agreements stemmed from personal connections instead of solid contracts. Moreover, Musk highlighted a petition advocating for Huang's return as CEO, stressing his invaluable influence in shaping Nvidia.
stories.bodyText:
Nvidia could lose some of its key supply chain agreements following Jensen Huang's departure, Tesla and SpaceX CEO 
Elon Musk
 has warned, pointing to the personal nature of several business arrangements made during the former chief executive's tenure.
Musk said Huang's ability to build and maintain relationships played an important role in securing deals for the chipmaker, with some agreements resting on personal assurances rather than written contracts.
Taking to X on Saturday, Musk said, "Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract."
He further cautioned that Huang's absence could affect these arrangements. "Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost," he added.
Musk's comments also come amid efforts to bring Huang back to the top job. On Friday, he publicly supported a petition seeking the former CEO's reinstatement. "A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I’m signing it too," Musk said in a post on X.
His support for Huang had also been evident earlier when a social media user suggested that Musk hire the Nvidia co-founder. 
Responding to the suggestion, Musk said, "That would be an honor."
Huang stepped down as Nvidia's president and chief executive officer amid growing scrutiny over reports of his alleged extramarital relationships.
The New York Times reported that Huang allegedly had a relationship with Nvidia Vice President of Healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports to him. The newspaper based its report on accounts from five people who had worked at the company.
The Wall Street Journal separately reported on Huang's alleged relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman suspected by some US intelligence officials of having links to Chinese intelligence services.
After Huang's resignation, Nvidia appointed its chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO as it begins the search for a permanent successor.
Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and remained at its helm for more than three decades. During this period, he oversaw the company's growth into one of the world's leading suppliers of artificial intelligence chips.
Musk's warning centres on the business relationships established during Huang's leadership, suggesting that his departure could have consequences beyond the change at the top. The Tesla CEO has specifically pointed to supply chain agreements that were built on his personal assurances rather than formal written commitments.

stories.headline: Faith, pollution and politics: How Yamuna takes centre stage every Chhath Puja
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Purity, hygiene and cleanliness are paramount for devotees during 
Chhath Puja
. With God as their witness - quite literally in this case - devotees go to great lengths to observe strict hygiene while following elaborate rituals centred around the worship of the Sun deity over four days.
In Delhi, however, devotees will step into the sullied waters of the Yamuna, believing that their faith will protect them.
As Delhi is already gasping for breath after Diwali, the debate has now pivoted to the pollution of the river which Delhi, for most of the year, views from the bridges built over it.
As thousands of people come down to the Yamuna's banks, the river will undergo its annual public audit by devotees standing waist-deep in its waters.
Significance of Chhath
Chhath Puja, rooted in devotion to the Sun God and Chhathi Maiya, is primarily observed by people from Bihar, eastern UP and Jharkhand.
Observed over four days, the festival begins with Nahay-Khay, when devotees prepare simple, traditional food while observing strict personal hygiene and purity.
This is followed by Kharna, when jaggery-based kheer and wheat rotis are prepared as prasad.
After Kharna, devotees undertake a rigorous 36-hour nirjala fast, abstaining from both food and water. 
The rituals culminate in offerings of arghya to the setting Sun, followed by prayers to the rising Sun on the final day.
Chhath and politics go hand in hand in Delhi
Every year, as Chhath Puja approaches, the Yamuna becomes more than a river for Delhi.
This year, BJP MP Manoj Tiwari took a dip in the Yamuna at Sonia Vihar, praising the cleanup under chief minister Rekha Gupta.
“How can we not appreciate the work that has been done here?” he said. “There might be crocodiles in the water here, but crocodiles come in clean water.”
AAP MLA Kuldeep Kumar answered by floating an effigy of Tiwari at Kalindi Kunj and challenging him to bathe there, claiming that stretch was far more polluted.
On Nahay Khay, the first day of the festival, a video purportedly showing dead fish near Sonia Vihar surfaced on social media.
Delhi ministers accused AAP of staging it, alleging that party workers bought fish from the market and dumped them in the river.
Delhi AAP chief Saurabh Bharadwaj denied this and demanded an inquiry on Friday, saying water samples had not yet been collected to establish the cause.
The river has been a political flashpoint around Chhath before. Last year, AAP alleged that a temporary artificial pool at Vasudev Ghat was built to project a clean Yamuna ahead of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s planned Chhath visit, which did not take place.
Why Chhath has become a political event
Chhath's growing political importance has a lot to do with Delhi's changing demography. According to reports, continued migration from Bihar, Jharkhand and eastern UP has increased the share of the Purvanchali community to about 30 percent of Delhi's population.
The festival offers political parties an opportunity to reach a sizeable constituency through a celebration deeply woven into its cultural identity.
According to reports, the Delhi government is setting up 1,482 Chhath ghats across 996 locations. The growing prominence of a festival once largely observed within community networks reflects how it has become an important fixture on the capital's political calendar.
Why the Yamuna turns frothy around Chhath
The Yamuna's pollution becomes particularly visible around Chhath Puja, when devotees gather in large numbers along its banks to offer prayers.
While talking to the Times of India, environmentalist Saumya Dutta said that the timing of Chhath coincides with a period when the river's flow has receded considerably after the monsoon, leaving less water to dilute the pollutants entering it.
“During the days of Chhath Puja, tens of thousands of Delhi residents from Bihar and eastern UP, along with others, add huge amounts of pollutants, particularly detergents containing surfactants, which are common ingredients in soaps and detergents, as well as some industrial waste,” Dutta said.
“Long after the peak monsoon flow, this is the period when the Yamuna's flow becomes very low. This low water flow, combined with high amounts of surfactants, causes large amounts of foam when the water is agitated. This becomes particularly visible during the huge influx of people and pollutants into this short 2% stretch of the Yamuna,” he said.
According to Dutta, the 22-km stretch through the capital accounts for roughly 2% of the Yamuna's total length but contributes 70-80% of its overall pollution load.
“Defaming agents and pre-Chhath cleaning do help for a very short period, but as the incoming pollution does not go down, this benefit is very short-term and vanishes quickly,” Dutta told TOI.
“The major reason for the abject failure of Yamuna cleaning plans, as well as schemes like Namami Gange, is that the huge daily inflow of partially treated or even untreated sewage and industrial effluent into the river is not being tackled,” he added.
The health risks for the devotees
In one of the most polluted major rivers of India, devotees will stand waist-deep, waiting for the Sun to set and rise the following day.
But is it safe for a person to come in contact with such polluted river?
According to Dr Srijan Garg immersion during Chhath can expose people to harmful bacteria, viruses and parasites through the skin, eyes, nose and ears, and sometimes through accidental ingestion.
"Devotees are exposed through the skin, eyes, nose, ear and sometimes by ingestion. However, the major exposure is through the skin and can cause various infections such as folliculitis, dermatitis, fungal infections," Dr. Garg told TOI.
The water is full of untreated sewage water. so swallowing that water will affect the health of the individual. Some acute infections typhoid, hepatitis A or E, giardiasis, cholera. These usually present with diarrhoea, vomiting and pain abdomen," he added.
Meanwhile, Dr. Ishan Singh said that people with cuts or open wounds are particularly vulnerable to infections.
"Industrial discharge may introduce heavy metals such as lead, mercury, arsenic and cadmium into river water. Depending on concentration and duration of exposure, these can affect the kidneys, liver and nervous system. Some chemicals may also irritate the skin and eyes," Dr. Singh told TOI.

"However, their actual presence and concentration at individual ghats must be confirmed through laboratory testing. A single brief exposure should not automatically be considered a cause of heavy-metal poisoning," he added.
He also said that children, pregnant women, elderly people, diabetic patients and people with weakened immunity need particular attention.
Dr. Singh also advised devotees to avoid swallowing river water, keep immersion time short and stay away from areas close to sewage discharge points. Those with open wounds should preferably avoid entering the water. After immersion, devotees should wash thoroughly with clean water and soap and change out of wet clothes.

stories.headline: U.S. must respect India’s right to defend itself, maintain zero tolerance towards terrorism: Blinken
stories.deck: “India is a global force,” Mr. Blinken said, adding that the relationship and shared interests between Washington and New Delhi were “really global in nature”
stories.bodyText:
The U.S. must respect India's right to defend itself and should maintain a zero-tolerance policy towards terrorism, former U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken said on Saturday (November 14, 2026), while describing Washington’s ties with New Delhi and Islamabad as “fundamentally different".
“India is a global force,” Mr. Blinken said, adding that the relationship and shared interests between Washington and New Delhi were “really global in nature”.
In contrast, the U.S. relationship with Pakistan is “regional," he said during a conversation with Jawed Ashraf, chairman of the India Trade Promotion Organisation, at a summit in New Delhi.
“The relations with Pakistan are regional, and there are still going to be important areas where we need to do things with them, particularly, for example, when it comes to counter-terrorism, but these are fundamentally different relationships,” he said.
“We have to have a zero-tolerance policy for terrorism. Period. And that means that we have to have respect for India's right to defend itself,” he added.
Mr. Blinken said the U.S. approach must include support for India’s efforts to respond to attacks as well as diplomatic efforts to prevent an escalation between New Delhi and Islamabad, the two nuclear-armed neighbours.
He added that efforts to prevent escalation were important given the destructive potential of the weapons both countries possess.
Reflecting on Washington's past engagement with Islamabad, Mr. Blinken said U.S. strategic interests during the Cold War and the war in Afghanistan may have led successive administrations to be less critical of Pakistan's civil-military establishment.
“And there's certainly an opportunity for the United States to do more,” he added.
On India-U.S. relations, Mr. Blinken described the transformation in ties over the past few decades as a shift from estrangement to a strategic partnership, underpinned by shared interests and people-to-people connections.
“We moved from estrangement to a genuine and, in some ways, unique partnership, built on a convergence of strategic interests. Of course, it is also underpinned by the profound people-to-people connections between our societies,” he said.
He identified cooperation in emerging technologies as an important area for the two countries, pointing to collaboration in space, quantum technology and artificial intelligence.
“The next step is tech cooperation, our ability to work in space, tech, quantum, and artificial intelligence,” he said.
On India’s relations with Russia, Mr. Blinken acknowledged the partnership's historical depth and said Washington did not expect New Delhi to sever those ties.
“There will be places where we don't have the same perspectives. For Russia, we understand there is deep history between India and Russia. So, we don't want them to end it,” he said.
Mr. Blinken, who served as the 71st Secretary of State from 2021 to 2025 under then-President Joe Biden, said the world was at a profound inflection point, citing rapid technological change, inequality and shifting power.
“The speed and profundity of change is beyond anything we've seen, certainly in my lifetime,” he said, noting that ChatGPT, an Artificial Intelligence (AI) chatbot, took one month to reach 50 million users, compared with 75 years for the telephone.
He said the private sector increasingly drove technological change, while governments struggled to keep pace. Growing inequalities had fuelled a sense among younger people that they were being “left out, left behind", he said.
Mr. Blinken warned that the U.S. risked weakening its strength by damaging cooperation between the government, universities and research institutions, and by becoming less welcoming to skilled people from abroad.
“The biggest danger I think we face is a huge self-inflicted wound,” he said.
On U.S. domestic politics, Mr. Blinken said the recent midterm results went beyond the usual setback for the party of a sitting President. He attributed the outcome partly to frustration over the cost of living and concerns about corruption.
In the November 3 midterm elections, the Democratic Party won majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, shifting control of the US Congress away from Republicans.
Mr. Blinken described the U.S.-Israeli military campaign against Iran, launched in February by President Donald Trump, as “a war of choice" and said the first Trump administration’s withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear agreement with Tehran had contributed to the crisis.
He said the agreement, signed in 2015 and formally known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), required Iran to ship out 97% of its enriched uranium and placed limits on its centrifuges, while allowing extensive inspections.
After the U.S. withdrawal from JCPOA in 2018, Iran accelerated its nuclear programme, Blinken added, saying the ongoing military action would not resolve the issue.
“It is very hard to try to force this Iranian regime to capitulate; it is possible to get it to negotiate. And these are very different things,” he said.
He called for an “off-ramp” to the conflict, warning that escalation could involve attacks on regional infrastructure, US bases and partner countries.
The Strait of Hormuz, he said, had become a major challenge for global energy supplies after not being a problem before the war. Since February, Iran has repeatedly restricted access to the narrow chokepoint, one of the world's busiest oil shipping channels.
On the wider West Asia conflict, Mr. Blinken said a lasting settlement required resolving the Palestinian question and establishing a sovereign Palestinian state alongside a secure Israel.
“There are seven million Jews in Israel. There are seven million Arabs and Palestinians between Israel proper, the West Bank and Gaza. No one is going anywhere despite what extremists on both sides would like to see happen," he said.
"The solution remains, I fully believe, even though this is not a popular view, a secure Israel and a sovereign state of Palestine," he added.

stories.headline: SpaceX makes history with successful rocket catch in Texas
stories.deck: SpaceX Makes History With Successful Rocket Catch in Texas
stories.bodyText: Starbase, Texas: SpaceX's giant Starship spacecraft pulled off a remarkable feat on Saturday afternoon in the quest to build fully reusable rockets. For the first time, the spacecraft successfully returned from orbit to its launch site in South Texas, where it was caught between two mechanical arms on the launch tower. . For the past decade, SpaceX has successfully landed the boosters of its smaller Falcon 9 rockets and then reused them on subsequent launches. But the upper stages of the Falcon 9s are still thrown away each time. . The Starship rocket system is not only much larger than Falcon 9, but it was designed from the start to be fully reusable. Bringing back an upper stage from orbit is a major technical hurdle, and SpaceX was able to pull it off on its first try. .Google executive Donald Harrison resigns from SpaceX board. Jared Isaacman, the NASA administrator, offered his congratulations. "Making more believers by the day .one step closer to," he wrote on social media, adding an emoji of the moon and the American flag. Starship is slated to serve as one of two lander designs that will take astronauts to the surface of the moon as part of NASA's Artemis program. . Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, posted a video showing a view of Starship from below, part of the post-landing inspection. . A few hours earlier, the spacecraft, which is about 170 feet long, had been traveling at more than 17,000 mph at an altitude of 170 miles. Then, one of its engines fired briefly, nudging it out of orbit to begin its fall back to Earth. .SpaceX says potential Tesla merger would need Musk's approval. As Starship entered the atmosphere, the pressure and friction of air heated the belly of the spacecraft and slowed its velocity. When it reached the denser parts of the atmosphere, flaps at the front and back steered it as it passed over Mexico before returning to Starbase, SpaceX's facility at the southern tip of Texas. . With the final landing burn, Starship pivoted to a vertical position, hovered and then slid between the mechanical arms that gently closed around it. . This was the 15th test flight of Starship, a mission that began when it launched Friday afternoon. It was not a complete success. The bottom booster stage, known as Super Heavy, accomplished its main objective of pushing the upper-stage spacecraft through the densest part of the atmosphere and then dropped away. . SpaceX had hoped that it would be able to catch Super Heavy at the launchpad, much as it did with the upper stage on Saturday. But as the booster headed back, it detected a problem and instead performed a simulated landing over the Gulf of Mexico. SpaceX is still investigating what happened. . The Starship spacecraft continued to orbit and deployed 26 of the company's next-generation Starlink satellites. . The words "DON'T PANIC" were printed on the side of the spacecraft, a reference to Douglas Adams' "The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy." This particular ship was No. 42 off the production line, and in Adams' book, 42 was the answer to the ultimate question of life, the universe and everything. . After about 22 hours and 14 orbits, Starship then returned to Earth. . Unlike Friday, when the skies over Starbase were cloudless and filled with sunshine, Saturday was cool, breezy and gray. In the final seconds, the spacecraft dropped through the clouds, and its engines fired one more time to pivot to vertical, hover and slide between the chopstick arms. . Now that Flight 15 has ended with a successful catch in Texas, Flight 16 could be the first Starship launch from SpaceX's revamped launchpad at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. . The Starbase launch site is not sufficient to serve SpaceX's planned acceleration of Starship launches. Another Florida launchpad is under construction at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, and SpaceX has announced plans to build a huge launch complex in Louisiana. . SpaceX could also hit a major milestone next year if it can launch two Starships in quick succession, dock them together in orbit and then move liquid methane and liquid oxygen propellants from one Starship to the other. . This refueling maneuver is essential for Starship to leave low-Earth orbit. Without it, the spacecraft could not make it to the moon for NASA, or head to more distant destinations like Mars, where Musk hopes to send people someday. . SpaceX's Starship is also slated to participate in its first NASA mission in the second half of next year. That flight, known as Artemis III, will stay in low-Earth orbit, where Starship will practice docking with NASA's Orion crew capsule. . In the original mission design, Starship and Orion were to travel separately to lunar orbit and dock there. But SpaceX wants the two spacecraft to dock in low-Earth orbit and then have Starship provide the propulsion to get them to the moon.

briefs.headline: U.S. air travel should recover from ground stop by end of November 15, FAA says
briefs.deck: New technology being added to the nation's air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the flight shutdown of more than four hours, Trump administration officials said
briefs.bodyText:
U.S. air travel should be fully recovered from the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years by the end of Sunday, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said on Saturday (November 14, 2026).
Mr. Bedford said the flights “will still have delays and cancellations” on Saturday (November 14) but promised that the “worst is behind us.”
His comments came as airlines across the U.S. worked to recover from a ground stoppage that lasted four hours, stranding hundreds of thousands of passengers.
New technology being added to the nation's air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the flight shutdown of more than four hours, Trump administration officials said.
Planes were taking flight and landing on Saturday (November 14), Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said. But the effects could be felt for days. Officials say the system will likely return to normal in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.
The nationwide stop was the first since January 2023, when another key Federal Aviation Administration computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the September 11, 2001, attacks.
Andrew Charlton, an aviation consultant, said Friday's (November 13) stoppage affected about a quarter of the 45,000 flights in the U.S. each day.
“The knock-on effect of that is incredible,” said Mr. Charlton, managing director of Aviation Advocacy. “The aircraft doesn't just fly from A to B and back to B and then stop. It then moves onto C and then over to E and around and around and around. It is, of course, exacerbated if you're talking about long-haul flights, international flights over the Atlantic or over the Pacific.”
Thousands of flights delayed and cancelled
At airports, passengers stared at screens showing delays or rushed to find buses or trains to their destinations.
Emily Brown and her 14-year-old daughter waited more than four hours on Friday (November 13) at the Dallas airport for their flight to Columbus, Ohio, before giving up. They were travelling to surprise her daughter's best friend. Instead, she had to settle for phoning the friend through tears in the airport, Ms. Brown said.
“She saved up her money to buy her own ticket, and she's planned this whole weekend,” Ms. Brown said. “Now we're not sure when we're gonna be able to go.”
A cheerful Southwest Airlines gate agent greeted passengers at Dallas Love Field at dawn on Saturday (November 14) with, “Good morning, good morning,” then repeatedly said all flights were full and asked passengers to have boarding passes ready to expedite the process and help keep flights moving.
Sports teams scheduled to play this weekend adjusted game start times, searched for hotel rooms, rescheduled flights and chartered buses. No. 19 Mississippi's game at Oklahoma was delayed a full day to Sunday (November 15). Start times for some other games were pushed back hours.
FlightAware, a website that tracks flights, said more than 4,100 flights had been cancelled. Cirium, a similar site, put that number above 3,200 flights.
Corbyn Wascher's flight was on the tarmac at the Charlotte, N.C., airport for four hours on Friday (November 13) on his way home to Moline, Illinois, from a conference in Miami. The 37-year-old high school teacher paid $100 to take an Uber to a hotel 25 minutes from the airport after he was unable to find a flight until Saturday (November 14) afternoon to Chicago.
At London's Heathrow Airport, several flights to and from the U.S. were listed as delayed or cancelled on Saturday (November 14).
“While U.S. flights have resumed, there may be some follow-on disruption as airlines work to rebook affected passengers and get all services back to normal,” said Tim Johnson, consumer director at the U.K. Civil Aviation Authority.
‘No one in danger during ground stop’
Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that no one was in any danger as more than 3,000 flights in the air at the time of the grounding order landed safely.
Mr. Duffy blamed Congress for failing to approve more funding for new technology, while downplaying the fact that trying to implement new fixes overtaxed the system. He suggested more disruptions might occur.
“We didn't think we would have this kind of outage. We did,” he said. “We were able to review what went wrong, and then reboot the system and go. But, you will have more of these.”
Mr. Duffy said the failure involved old equipment and was not linked to the FAA's new AI-powered system, which the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky.
The problem was due to updating a system that can never shut down, Mr. Charlton said.
“What you're watching here is trying to change the tires of your car when the car's going at 80 miles an hour down the expressway, because nothing stops in aviation,” Mr. Charlton said. “It's a 24/7 operation. And to make changes on the fly, if you'll pardon that pun, is incredibly complex and dangerous.”
The FAA already replaced thousands of old copper wires with fibre optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding. Mr. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
Past problem linked to equipment failures
The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, although that disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fibre optic line. Ageing equipment was also blamed for brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference this time was the nationwide scale of the disruption, which left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.
“If you don't have that ability, whether it's because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you've got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you're going to risk not being able to communicate with them,” said Mr. Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.
It differed from the one after 9/11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Mr. Arroyo said.

briefs.headline: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from moving ahead on Washington public golf course redevelopment
briefs.deck: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued the temporary restraining order before the East Potomac Golf Links was due to close on November 15 for 15 months
briefs.bodyText:
A federal judge on Saturday (November 14, 2026) ordered a temporary stop to any work at a historic Washington public golf course not far from the White House, blocking for now President Donald Trump's push to redevelop the site along the Potomac River into a championship-level venue.
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued the temporary restraining order before the East Potomac Golf Links was due to close on Sunday (November 15) for 15 months. Mr. Trump had announced work would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.
The plaintiffs argue that Mr. Trump's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something the Republican president denies. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would "irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest."
The park's redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation's capital that Mr. Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Centre for the Performing Arts, among others.
Ms. Reyes had signalled throughout a five-hour court hearing on Friday (November 13) that she was likely to issue a stoppage order for the park closure. The only issue was how expansive it might be. Justice Department lawyer Adam Gustafson argued that the entire East Potomac Park, which includes three golf courses, a miniature course, bike-riding lanes, and other recreational areas, was being closed for safety reasons. He also noted that the lease between the government and the current operator, National Links Trust, was ending on Sunday (November 15).
Ms. Reyes pointed out that safety had not been part of the discussion over the closure for months and that ending the lease felt more like an action that provided a premise for the closure rather than an action that led to the closure of the course about 2 miles from the White House.
She also rejected Gustafson's argument that the closure was separate from Mr. Trump's repeated pronouncements that he wanted the course to be closed and renovated into a world-class venue and had called repeatedly for the park's closure by the deadline as part of what is known as the Washington National plan.
Even before the order, Mr. Trump lashed out in a social media post on Saturday (November 14), contending that Reyes "doesn't want us to quickly and inexpensively fix up the Course which is also very dangerous." He said people who live in the Washington area would get a 50 per cent discount on "any Rates charged" and that the redevelopment would "evolve into something very special, something which the Judge will be able to take great pride in seeing!"
Ms. Reyes' order was the latest in a series of rulings in lawsuits challenging Mr. Trump's projects that were issued just hours before construction was expected to begin. A different judge recently ordered a 14-day delay on work for the arch, a decision that came shortly after a key planning commission stacked with Mr. Trump appointees approved plans for the project.
Ms. Reyes, who was nominated to the court by Democratic President Joe Biden, had for months been reticent about approving the plaintiffs' requests for work stoppages. The plaintiffs had argued the administration was moving ahead with work related to the project despite the pending lawsuit.
Her reluctance to issue orders ended in October, spurred in part by a tree-cutting spree by the administration over a holiday weekend with little notification to the judge or plaintiffs.
Officials and government lawyers said the tree work was part of a 2019 plan that recommended the cutting. In response, the judge confronted the administration over what she portrayed as deceitful actions over its intentions for the project.
Ms. Reyes has repeatedly expressed frustration over the minute planning details she has been asked to adjudicate, including over the trees being cut down at the 106-year-old park. The Justice Department filed a request that Reyes be removed from the case because of what it called her "egregious behaviour" and questioned her impartiality. Reyes has not recused herself.
The restraining order was one of two issues Reyes took up during Friday's (November 13) hearing.
She announced plans last week to name Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, to examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Justice Department had violated ethics or misled her during the course of the case. Mr. Gustafson asked her to reconsider and give the Justice Department the opportunity to show an outside investigator was unnecessary.
"It's quite a cloud on the people it affects," he said.
Ms. Reyes said she understood.
"To be frank with you I don't want to do this," she said, but she had an ethical obligation to at least look because "I think there is enough smoke that someone needs to consider whether there's been fire."

But last week, after winning the Booker Prize for his “destabilising and satirical dystopian novel”, The End of Everything, he said he had lost hope for humanity — even as people continued to fight to change the world. Did something change in seven years?
Harrison was born in 1945 and grew up in the shadow of the Second World War. He has said he was impressed by The Waste Land by T.S. briefs.headline: Prince William, Princess Kate to visit Mumbai for Earthshot Prize Awards; gully cricket, Metro ride, Bollywood on itinerary

briefs.bodyText:
Prince William and Catherine, the Princess of Wales, will visit Mumbai from November 16 to 18 for the sixth annual Earthshot Prize Summit and Awards Night, with a three-day itinerary featuring engagements focused on environmental sustainability, gully cricket, public transport and India’s film industry.
The visit will mark the royal couple’s second official trip to India. According to a statement issued ahead of the visit, the Prince and Princess will participate in several engagements across Mumbai aimed at highlighting innovation, youth leadership and cultural ties between India and the United Kingdom.
The couple will begin their engagements on Monday (November 16, 2026), with an event celebrating Mumbai’s tradition of gully cricket and the shared passion for the sport in India and the U.K.
Later in the day, Prince William will travel on the Mumbai Metro to highlight the importance of sustainable urban transport. He will also attend the Earthshot Prize Impact Assembly, where discussions will focus on scaling solutions to major environmental challenges.
On Tuesday (November 17, 2026), the Prince will meet the 2026 Earthshot Prize finalists before joining Princess Kate for the inaugural Children’s Earthshot Awards Ceremony at the Museum of Solutions.
The children’s awards follow a nationwide programme involving 15,000 schools across 24 Indian states, which invited children aged nine to 17 to develop solutions to environmental problems affecting their communities.
The couple will attend the Earthshot Prize Awards Night later that evening. The annual environmental initiative recognises five winners working on solutions to challenges including climate change, air pollution, waste management, ocean conservation and biodiversity loss. Each winner receives £1 million to support their work.
India has produced more Earthshot Prize winners and finalists than any other country, according to the statement.
On Wednesday (November 18, 2026), the couple will visit an institution dedicated to traditional craftsmanship to learn how preserving craft techniques can contribute to sustainable textile production.
Princess Kate will also visit a maternity hospital in Mumbai, where she will interact with healthcare professionals and families to understand approaches to maternal healthcare and support during the earliest stages of family life.
The royal couple will conclude their visit at Dharma Productions, where they will learn about India’s film industry and its global cultural influence. The engagement will also highlight the longstanding creative connections between India and the United Kingdom.
Princess Kate’s attendance at the Earthshot Prize Awards Night will be her first since the ceremony was held in Boston in 2022.

briefs.headline: Benjamin Netanyahu calls for Israeli unity government, Eisenkot dismisses ‘tricks’
briefs.deck: The latest exchange comes as Mr,. Eisenkot is in the midst of negotiations to form a government, after he was tapped for the post of premier on Nov. 15, 2026
briefs.bodyText:
Israel’s caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday (November 14, 2026) reiterated his calls for a national unity government with his opponent Gadi Eisenkot, who in turn dismissed the appeal as a ruse.
The latest exchange comes as Mr,. Eisenkot is in the midst of negotiations to form a government, after he was tapped for the post of premier on Sunday (November 15, 2026).
A meeting with Mr. Eisenkot on Thursday (November 13, 2026) “only strengthened the conviction that it is essential to form a national unity government” to guarantee Israel’s security, Mrx. Netanyahu said in a video statement, adding that such a government could “eliminate the Iranian threat once and for all”.
He said this government would be made up of parties that recognise Israel “as a state for the Jewish people”.
It would address security challenges, he added, most notably Iran which he claimed would “not hesitate to use nuclear weapons against us”.
The outgoing Prime Minister warned against Mr. Eisenkot’s plan to form a minority government, presented as a “national emergency government”.
Such a plan would see the 48 lawmakers in Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc vote in favour of his government, against the 46 Netanyahu backers. The 26 other members of parliament, from Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties, could abstain, allowing the government to be approved without an absolute majority in the Knesset, which has 120 seats.
“Instead of trying to form a weak and dangerous government... let’s meet in one room, without preconditions, put aside all our disagreements and all the boycotts, and reach agreements for the security and the future of the state,” Mr Netanyahu urged.
Minutes later, Mr. Eisenkot responded by saying Mr. Netanyahu “knows he lost the election”, accusing him of playing “tricks” by appealing for a unity government.
“Netanyahu is calling for negotiations while they are already underway; he claims to want unity but... sows division and stokes tensions as if there were no tomorrow,” the former army chief said, adding that “these tricks don’t work on me”.
‘Break with extremists’
Mr. Eisenkot was tapped on Sunday (November 15, 2026) to form a new government within 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension.
Negotiations are expected to be difficult, especially as Netanyahu has waged a campaign to discredit Arab-Israeli parties, which gained a record number of seats in the election.
Mr. Netanyahu’s proposed unity government would be made up of key Jewish parties ranging from the centre to the right, while excluding the Arab parties.
Mr. Eisenkot has indicated he would be open to forming a government with members of Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party, as well as outgoing Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism, provided their commitment to unity is “sincere”.
But a unity government with Mr. Netanyahu himself remains unlikely, particularly after Mr. Eisenkot denounced his “racist” campaign against Arab parties on Friday.
Mr. Eisenkot on Saturday (November 14, 2026) reiterated his calls for a “break with the extremists”, notably supporters of far-right minister Itamar Ben Gvir, as a condition for any participation in a government under his leadership.
Another point of contention is the election on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) of the Speaker of the Knesset, a post currently held by Amir Ohana, a close Mr. Netanyahu ally. The opposition has put forward Matan Kahana, a former officer in the Israeli army who was fifth on Gadi Eisenkot’s list, to replace him.
“If they (Likud and its allies) are truly seeking a sincere political partnership, as they claim, they must allow the democratic process to unfold normally... and instruct their members of parliament to support the appointment of Matan Kahana,” Mr. Eisenkot said.

stories.headline: Karnataka CM DK Shivakumar seeks 9th Schedule SC-ST quota cover
stories.deck: Chief Minister D K Shivakumar has written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi regarding reservation provisions for SCs and STs. The Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes Act, 2022, aims to enhance reservation quotas in education and employment. The High Court ruled against the increased reservations, raising concerns regarding the 50% ceiling limitation. Shivakumar emphasized the need for a…
stories.bodyText:
BENGALURU: Chief minister 
D K Shivakumar
 has written to 
PM Narendra Modi
, urging him to bring about a constitutional amendment to include Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes Act, 2022, in Ninth Schedule of the Constitution, thereby protecting its provision of reservations for SCs and STs in education and public employment.
The law raised reservation for SCs from 15% to 17% and for STs from 3% to 7%, taking the overall quota to 56% in the state. It followed recommendations by a commission headed by retired Karnataka high court judge Justice H N Nagamohan Das.
On Oct 12, 2026, HC struck down the enhanced reservation provisions, ruling that the aggregate quota exceeded the 50% ceiling. Clarifying govt’s position, Shivakumar said the issues flagged by HC called for a constitutional solution and shouldn’t result in abandon-ing SC-ST communities’ aspirations for educational and employment opportunities.
Shivakumar said Karnataka’s proposal predated high court verdict, having been submitted to Union govt on March 23, 2023.
CM: K’taka’s plea must get same attention as TN’s case
Citing Tamil Nadu’s 69% reservation framework, which was included in the Ninth Schedule through the Constitution (76th Amendment) Act, 1994, he wrote: “If Parliament could act to protect a reservation framework of 69% in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka’s request for 56% reservation, founded on the recommendations of a judicial commission, deserves no less constitutional attention.”
The legislative assembly passed a resolution seeking Ninth Schedule protection on Dec 18, 2025, while former chief minister Siddaramaiah reiterated the demand in a letter to Modi on April 16, 2026.
In a Lok Sabha reply on July 25, 2026, the Union govt acknowledged receiving the proposal, but said Ninth Schedule inclusion was not appropriate while the matter was pending before the court.
Following the high court verdict, Shivakumar urged the Centre not to defer consideration on account of the ongoing appellate proceedings.
He sought consultations with the National Commissions for SCs and STs and a time-bound examination by the ministries of law and justice, social justice and empowerment, tribal affairs, and home affairs.
Karnataka, he said, was ready to provide empirical material and address the constitutional and procedural issues identified by the court.

briefs.headline: Target-100: Karnataka government ramps up efforts to improve SSLC, II pre-university exam score
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: The school education department has launched a series of district-level interactive programmes with teachers and officials to strengthen preparations for the upcoming SSLC and II PUC examinations and improve pass percentages.
The initiative began in Dharwad Friday, where the district has set a target of ensuring that every student scores above 60%, with a 100% pass rate. Dubbed ‘Target-60’, the goal is an improvement over last academic year’s target of 40%. Officials said targets would vary across districts.
Teachers have been asked to focus on model question papers, question banks for lesson-based assessments (LBAs) and board examination blueprints. A student tracking system will monitor individual performance from LBAs and Summative Assessment 1 to the ongoing preparatory examinations.
“Every Saturday, headmasters and teachers will analyse students’ performance and work collectively to improve outcomes. Meetings at the BEO and DDPI levels will be held fortnightly, while deputy commissioners will review progress once a month. The focus is on reaching the last child,” said Rashmi V Mahesh, additional chief secretary, department of School Education.
Initiatives such as buddy pairing and morning alarm bells will continue. The department will also raise awareness about the rural quota reservation coming into effect this year and motivate students to explore higher education opportunities.
Addressing concerns over absenteeism, Mahesh said although many students registered for exams last year, a significant number did not appear for either the preparatory or final exams. Parent-teacher meetings (PTMs) will be held this year, with teachers asked to visit students’ homes if parents do not attend school, to stress the importance of appearing for exams.
School education minister Madhu Bangarappa said the absence of nearly 60,000 students from last year’s examinations was a concern, but cautioned against holding teachers solely responsible. “Personal and family-related problems faced by children could also have been responsible,” he said.
Crediting teachers’ efforts, including special classes and additional learning support, for Karnataka’s record pass percentages of 98.08% in SSLC and 92.25% in II PUC last academic year, Bangarappa said teachers must now work towards achieving a 100% pass rate.

briefs.headline: Bengaluru’s taxi operators seek cap on Green SM fleet, flag threat to livelihoods
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Private transport associations have opposed the proposed entry of Vietnam-based Green SM, an electric taxi service operated by Vingroup, arguing that its company-owned fleet could threaten the livelihoods of thousands of independent taxi and autorickshaw operators.
In a representation to the chief minister, the Federation of Karnataka State Private Transport Associations said individual drivers purchase vehicles through bank or non-banking financial company (NBFC) loans and bear expenses such as EMIs, insurance, permits, maintenance and fuel. Since their earnings depend on the number of trips they make each day, they remain particularly vulnerable to fluctuations in demand.
The federation argued that Green SM would have an advantage through access to corporate capital, bulk vehicle purchases, its own app and fleet-management systems. These resources, it said, could allow the company to sustain losses for longer and offer fares that individual operators would struggle to match.
It also questioned reports of fares starting at Rs 8 per km, arguing that such rates could be below actual operating costs. 
The federation warned that smaller operators could be forced to lower fares, default on loan repayments or exit the market. Estimating that nearly eight lakh Bengaluru families depend on the autorickshaw and taxi sector, it has sought a cap of 100 vehicles on Green SM’s fleet, an audit of its licence compliance and scrutiny of its fare structure.
Meanwhile, commuters have taken to social media, calling for more transport operators and lower fares. Several users argued that increased competition would benefit passengers. “Autorickshaw drivers usually do not come in the direction of our ride. Even if they agree to come, they do not switch on the meter. More cab operators is always better for the city,” one user commented.
Another user said the opposition was driven by commercial interests rather than commuters’ concerns: “The current controversy is market-driven. Those already in the business do not want another player to enter.”

briefs.headline: Schoolkids when work began, professionals when Metro opened: A decade-long wait ends as Bengaluru’s Pink Line opens
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 For many residents along Bannerghatta Road, the opening of Pink Line Metro marked the end of a nearly decade-long wait. Having watched the corridor take shape from their schooldays into adulthood, they finally got to experience the service Saturday morning as commercial operations between Kalena Agrahara and SG Palya began at 6am.
Among the early passengers were Aditya and Yash, who said they were school students when Bangalore Metro Rail Corporation Ltd (BMRCL) began construction. “We grew up watching the construction work on Bannerghatta Road. We were in school when the project began, and could take our first ride only after starting our careers,” Yash said.
For Aditya, a Metro enthusiast, the line’s launch has also raised hopes of better citywide connectivity. “BMRCL should prioritise opening the remaining stretches of Pink Line and commissioning the Blue Line. Metro services will ease road congestion and encourage people to shift from private vehicles to public transport,” he said.
College student Vibhor Mandal, meanwhile, said the journey brought back childhood memories. “I was in class 4 when construction began. I’m now in college. I came here out of curiosity, to experience the service after watching the work for so many years,” he said.
Construction of Pink Line began in 2017, with completion initially scheduled for 2021-22. However, the project missed several deadlines, partly because the previous contractor, Simplex, failed to execute the work as per contractual terms.
As services began Saturday, BMRCL security personnel welcomed passengers with smiles and roses. Greater Bengaluru development minister Krishna Byre Gowda also travelled from Kalena Agrahara to SG Palya, interacting with commuters. Women dressed in pink added to the celebratory mood, while some parents brought their children along for the ride.
A woman passenger said the new line had brought relief to residents who earlier depended on the Green and Yellow lines. “Our first ride on Pink Line will always remain special. We waited years for it to open, and it is now much closer to our residential areas,” she said.
Byre Gowda said passengers were happy with the launch and officials had been instructed to ensure smooth operations. He added that Pink Line is expected to boost ridership on the Yellow Line, which connects to Electronics City. An additional train is to be deployed on Yellow Line this week to improve frequency.
With the launch of Pink Line, Jayadeva Interchange station, connecting the Pink and Yellow lines, is now fully operational. However, commuters said transfers between the lines were challenging and sought better signage.
7.5km in 10 minutes
For residents accustomed to Bannerghatta Road’s traffic congestion, the Metro offered an immediate glimpse of the difference it could make to daily commutes.
Dinesh, who travelled on the new line, said the journey between Kalena Agrahara and SG Palya took just 10 minutes. “It takes around 40 minutes by road to cover the 4km from Kalena Agrahara to JP Nagar, where I work. The Metro has brought huge relief to residents here,” he said. Fares range from Rs 10 to Rs 30, depending on distance.
Residents said they had endured years of pothole-ridden roads, dust and traffic diversions, particularly during the construction of Jayadeva Interchange station. The start of Metro services was therefore a welcome change after prolonged disruption and inconvenience.
Opening tunnel section
Despite celebrating the elevated stretch’s opening, many commuters said commissioning the underground section would bring greater benefits.
Santosh M, a techie working on Outer Ring Road, said his journey between Kalena Agrahara and SG Palya took 10 minutes, compared with at least 45 minutes by road on weekdays. “But opening the remaining Pink Line section should be the priority. Extending services at least up to MG Road in the next few months would significantly increase ridership and help those travelling to the central business district and Whitefield. Good last-mile connectivity and proper footpaths around stations are also equally important,” he said.
Another passenger, Krishna, said the underground section would considerably ease congestion on Bannerghatta Road. “Many are eagerly waiting for stations such as MG Road and Cantonment to open, as they will provide better connectivity and relief to commuters,” he said.
Responding to these demands, Byre Gowda said govt was working towards commissioning the remaining stretch in 7-8 months.
Bus info at station
For the first time, BMRCL has introduced a passenger information system displaying onward bus services and their estimated arrival times. At SG Palya station, information on buses heading towards KR Market, Majestic and the international airport, among other destinations, was displayed. BMTC has already announced five dedicated feeder services to connect to Pink Line Metro.
Chief minister 
DK Shivakumar
 travelled on the newly inaugurated Pink Line from Kalena Agrahara to SG Palya on the first day of commercial operations. Marking Children’s Day, he interacted with children and commuters, seeking feedback on the new Metro service.

briefs.headline: Remembrance Day service at St Mark’s Cathedral in Bengaluru on November 15
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Continuing a tradition rooted in its military heritage, St Mark’s Cathedral will host its annual Remembrance Day observance Sunday, bringing together war veterans, serving armed forces personnel, diplomats and members of the congregation to honour soldiers who laid down their lives in wars and conflicts.
Observed for over a century, Remembrance Day commemorates the end of hostilities on the Western Front during 
World War I
 on Nov 11, 1918. The Cathedral, which served as a garrison church for the British military before Independence, has maintained its association with the armed forces through an annual remembrance service held for the past two decades. The observance takes place on the Sunday closest to Nov 11.
This year’s programme will feature two services, including a special service inside the church, followed by a wreath-laying ceremony at a temporary cenotaph erected beside the Cathedral. Around 500 people are expected to attend, including a significant contingent of veterans from the 
Indian Armed Forces
.
“We are delighted and consider it a great privilege that war veterans have chosen St Mark’s Cathedral for this observance. It is a matter of immense pride and honour for us to host this solemn occasion,” said Rev D Theodore William, Presbyter-in-Charge of the Cathedral.
The service will pay tribute to personnel from the Army, Navy and Air Force who lost their lives in the two World Wars, subsequent military operations, counter-insurgency engagements and United Nations peacekeeping missions.
Anjana Samuel, secretary of the church, said the gathering would also bring together members of the diplomatic corps, serving and retired military personnel and the congregation.
The observance will also remember bereaved families and recognise the contributions and sacrifices of veterans and serving armed forces personnel.

briefs.headline: Dad’s plea after teen’s accident: Secure dupatta before riding pillion
briefs.deck: Praveen Borape's daughter Hetal suffered serious injuries when her dupatta caught in a two-wheeler's wheel. The fabric tightened around her neck, causing critical damage to her voice box. After complex surgery at Manipal Hospital in Bengaluru, Hetal regained her ability to speak. Her father urges parents to secure loose garments to prevent similar accidents. Strangulation injuries from clothing…
briefs.bodyText:
BENGALURU: For Praveen Borape, the sound of his 13-year-old daughter Hetal speaking again is nothing short of a miracle.
After months of uncertainty, the Pune-based family finally has reason to celebrate. But the ordeal has also left Praveen with an urgent message for fellow parents: Before taking your daughter on a two-wheeler, make sure her dupatta and other loose clothing are properly secured.
In May 2025, Hetal was travelling with her father on a two-wheeler to visit her uncle when her dupatta got caught in the vehicle’s rear wheel.
Within moments, the fabric tightened around her neck, strangulating her and causing severe injuries to her voice box and windpipe.
“Her dupatta got stuck in the wheel and, before we knew it, it was wrapped around her neck and strangulating her. We were in shock and rushed her to a nearby hospital for treatment. But my wife and I were worried whether our daughter would ever be able to speak again,” Praveen recalled.
In May 2026, the family approached Manipal Hospital, Old Airport Road, Bengaluru, where doctors identified the extensive damage to her airway and voice box.
Dr EV Raman, lead consultant, Children’s Airway and Swallowing Centre, ENT, said the strangulation had severely damaged Hetal’s larynx and windpipe, requiring complex surgical intervention.
The medical team performed a procedure called laryngotracheoplasty, in which the narrowed and damaged portion of the airway was removed and the healthy ends were rejoined.
A stent was placed to keep the reconstructed airway open, while a tracheostomy tube helped Hetal breathe during her recovery. The stent was to remain in place for six to 12 weeks before removal.
Dr Raman cautioned that strangulation injuries caused by loose garments getting caught in moving vehicle wheels can have devastating consequences.
“They can also leave behind wounds that heal poorly. Strangulation injuries can damage the voice box and airway, and in some cases, can be fatal. There is also a risk of blood entering the lungs. Reconstructing the damaged area requires extremely complex surgeries. 
These procedures are expensive and are performed at very few centres. This is why people need to be careful,” he said.
Following surgery and subsequent medical follow-ups, Hetal regained her ability to speak and breathe independently.
“Luckily, my daughter is healthy today. I urge parents to ensure that their children’s dupattas and other loose clothing are secured before taking them on two-wheelers,” he said.

briefs.headline: Milk, paneer prices pinch paying guest accommodation budgets; rents to rise in Bengaluru
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Steep increase in prices of milk products, especially the price of paneer, is prompting paying guest accommodations to consider increasing per-person rent by Rs 500 a month — a second such increase in four months.
Students and working professionals who stay in PGs will have to loosen their purse strings as PG owners have gone back to the drawing board doing maths on a likely rent revision. They argued that rental revisions are to cut losses and not to make profits.
A PG owner in Shanthinagar said it was a toss-up between higher rents and a cutback on what’s offered in a thali. For now, they serve paneer three days a week and milk and curd every day. The paths are clear: either reduce frequency and quantity or hike rents.
Another PG owner, who runs three units in Marathahalli, said expensive paneer was a key villain and hinted at a decision next week.
At present, basic beds in a PG cost Rs 5,000, average beds Rs 8,000 to Rs 9,000 and luxury PGs up to Rs 20,000. Arun Kumar DT, president of PG Welfare Association, said: “With work-from-home still an option in many companies, most PGs are running at about 70% of their capacity. 
We’ve to bear losses while maintaining the quality of food.”
Paying Guest Accommodation Welfare Association, Bangalore, recently announced a hike in rent effective August 1, citing that prices of essential commodities had gone up since March.
Rents went up by Rs 500 for three- and four-person rooms and by Rs 1,000 for one- and two-person rooms. The association cited higher costs of food supplies, cleaning material, salaries, electricity, water, gas and maintenance of fans, motors, lifts, generators and borewells. While a gas refill jumped from Rs 1,800 to Rs 3,300 in two months, a rice bag became costlier by Rs 400 and a cooking-oil box by Rs 500.
At the receiving end are working professionals like Lalitha R, who lives in a PG in Mahadevapura. She said the owners were planning to replace paneer with soya chunks. Another PG, according to her, has reduced the supply of curd to just once a day. “This is terrible,” she added.

briefs.headline: Bengaluru family murders: Did accused take victims’ thumbprints to claim property?
briefs.bodyText:
The police are now probing a property angle in the ghastly murder of seven persons of the same family in Rajajinagar, Bengaluru.
Cab driver-turned-YouTuber and tabloid editor Indushekhar allegedly killed his wife, mother-in-law, and family members of his brothers-in-law. He was assisted by his minor daughter. He allegedly claimed the family had been insulting him, pushing him to kill them. However, the police are now probing whether the accused took the thumb impressions of the deceased on stamp papers after he killed them. He is suspected of having collected the impressions to establish his claim over the property.
According to the police, the accused was allegedly eyeing a 30x40 site in Srirampura owned by his mother-in-law, Roopavathi.
The police suspect that Indushekhar’s minor daughter actively assisted him in the crime in the hope of inheriting the Srirampura property. Indushekhar had allegedly promised to transfer the house in her name, after which she agreed to help him, investigators suspect.
Luminol test
Meanwhile, forensic teams have collected scientific evidence from Indushekhar’s house, the scene of the crime. Investigators suspect that bloodstains from the hall, bathroom and the alleged murder weapon, a grinding stone, were wiped off after the killings.
A luminol test was conducted to identify traces of blood that may have remained despite the cleaning. The samples collected by the Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL) and Scene of Crime Officer (SOCO) teams have been sent for further examination.
Luminol is a forensic chemical that reacts with haemoglobin in blood and produces a blue glow, helping investigators detect possible blood traces that are invisible to the naked eye.

stories.headline: Anthropic’s valuation can’t secure its moat
stories.deck: Its engineers need to keep building progressively more capable models; the AI firm has also not established that it will be able to sustain its profitability after honouring its infra commitments
stories.bodyText:
Artificial intelligence (AI) company Anthropic, best known as the maker of the Claude AI model, is preparing to go public at a valuation of $1.4 trillion, which could make the IPO one of the largest in history. However, this particular refrain has of late seemed more ominous than cause for optimism, and the Anthropic IPO could be no exception.
The company has said it will offer 825 million shares at $70-78 apiece, to raise up to $64.4 billion. The valuation includes shares to be issued through employee options and other arrangements, and its market capitalisation based on outstanding shares is likely to be near $1 trillion. (It was valued at $965 billion in a private funding round in May.)
Anthropic’s financial prospects depend on continuing to spend extraordinary sums of money. Its amended prospectus filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on November 10 revealed roughly $900 billion in spending commitments, almost entirely for computing infrastructure, until 2045.
Of this, the company expects to incur half by 2030 and $70.7 billion in the twelve months from September 30. The filing also mentions another $150-175 billion in potential payments under arrangements sans fixed dollar commitments. Of this, the company expects to incur half by 2030 and $70.7 billion in the twelve months from September 30.
The filing also mentions another $150-175 billion in potential payments under arrangements sans fixed dollar commitments.
These figures clarify a colossal exposure to future demand that neither Anthropic nor other Big AI companies have thus far been able to guarantee.
And while Anthropic’s revenue has also been growing, from $2.5 billion in the first three quarters of 2025 to $33.2 billion in the corresponding slice of 2026, the proposed fully diluted valuation exceeds annualised sales 17-fold.
The current business model is, largely, to charge customers according to how many tokens they use to run their tasks on its AI models. From January to September 2026, this revenue constituted 79% of the total revenue, giving Anthropic a reason to encourage users to maximise token use, irrespective of changes in the value of the output generated — a tendency famously called tokenmaxxing. But three factors complicate this picture. First, Anthropic has said AI models released within the last six months accounted for more than 80% of its third quarter revenue, which means its engineers need to keep building progressively more capable models. Second, it has not established that it will be able to sustain its profitability after honouring its infrastructure commitments.
The third factor is the most important, however: neither Anthropic nor its competitors, including OpenAI, currently has a lasting competitive advantage, a.k.a. a moat.
In a recent study in the Journal of Economic Perspectives, researchers (including two affiliated with Amazon and Microsoft), reported that the price of AI inference of similar quality had fallen almost a thousandfold between late 2023 and late 2025, based on data from the OpenRouter marketplace. Given historical price rates, similar improvements would have taken computer storage two decades and lithium-ion batteries, five. The reasons include an explosion in the number of competing models, especially of the open-source variety, with customers being willing to pay less to use proprietary models as a result.
In one response, Anthropic sought to secure its access to computing infrastructure. Per the prospectus, it is committed to spending at least $47.2 billion with Microsoft until June 2033, $121.3 billion with Google until July 2033, and $110 billion with Amazon Web Services through April 2036. But while these deals help Anthropic secure its computing resources, the long-term payment obligations also exist in a market where customers can reduce spending much faster. This means Anthropic will have to generate demand just as fast to ensure it utilises the capacity it has already contracted for — even as better hardware and more efficient models periodically adjust the cost of providing AI services.
In fact, the difficulties of securing a moat are better illustrated by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s position of late, in favour of new regulatory and compliance demands. These demands could impose costs that larger AI companies will bear more easily than smaller ones.
Legitimate reasons
Legitimate reasons to regulate AI include security failures and the risks posed by autonomous systems but governments should endeavour overtly to prevent such regulatory capture given the perverse incentives facing AI companies.
Overall, neither Anthropic nor its competitors have presented evidence of a sturdy moat. Instead, thanks to capable open-source development, models are becoming cheaper and competitors are catching up, and efficiency gains threaten the pricing power on which their valuations depend.
