stories.headline: US diesel prices retreat, fall below $6 per gallon for first time in two months
stories.deck: US diesel prices have dropped below $6 per gallon for the first time in two months. This decline comes after prices surged to an all-time high in September due to global supply issues. Lower diesel prices are providing some relief to consumers, businesses, and farmers who have faced increased costs recently. Along with diesel prices, gasoline prices have also decreased, falling below $4 per…
stories.bodyText:
US diesel prices have falled below the $6 level for the first time in two months. It has eased some of the pressure on consumers, farmers and businesses following a sharp increase triggered by disruptions to global oil supplies.
The national average retail price fell to $5.998 per gallon on Saturday, according to fuel price tracker GasBuddy, cited by Reuters. The decline comes after diesel touched an all-time high of $6.519 on September 22, with prices briefly crossing $10 per gallon in California.
The surge had become a wider economic concern because diesel is central to the transportation and freight industry. Higher fuel costs pushed up expenses for businesses and farmers, while adding to inflationary pressures on households. Fuel prices also became a major political issue, contributing to voter dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump's Republicans ahead of this month's midterm elections, which saw Democrats sweep both houses of Congress.
The earlier price rally was driven by supply disruptions linked to the US-Israeli war against Iran and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. Washington's efforts to contain the increase, including temporarily lifting federal taxes on red-dyed diesel, easing sanctions on Russian fuel and announcing an $8 billion support programme for farmers, offered limited relief.
The latest retreat comes amid a combination of softer crude prices and seasonal changes in fuel consumption. Brent crude futures have dropped 18.5 per cent over the past two weeks, while demand for diesel typically weakens during autumn as travel slows and hurricane-related risks to Gulf Coast refineries decline.
Refinery output is also recovering as scheduled maintenance is largely completed by November, Patrick De Haan, GasBuddy's head of petroleum analysis, said.
The easing in fuel costs is not limited to diesel. Average US gasoline prices also fell below $4 per gallon this month for the first time since August 10, GasBuddy data showed.

stories.headline: Strong economy drives NH toll to record Rs 6,640 crore in October
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Toll collection on national highways and expressways touched an all-time high of around Rs 6,640 crore in Oct, indicating stronger economic activity and increased movement of vehicles across the country's highway network.
The collection of user fee was around 16% higher than the Rs 5,715 crore recorded in Oct 2025. The previous highest monthly toll revenue was Rs 6,185 crore, collected in May this year. Going by the trend, the total toll collection is projected to be around Rs 74,000 crore, officials said.
A significant change was also visible in the mode of payment, with cash collections dropping sharply to barely Rs 4 crore last month from Rs 84 crore in the corresponding month last year. At the same time, payments through the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) rose to around Rs 100 crore in Oct, against no such collection a year ago.
The sharp decline in cash transactions follows govt directions to move away from cash payments for highway user fees and use FASTag or UPI as the default modes for paying the user charge. Officials said stricter monitoring was being carried out to ensure that cash is completely phased out as a mode of toll payment. "End of cash transaction will eliminate any scope of malpractices. More people are also opting for FASTag Annual Passes, which is a good sign," said another official. Growing adoption of electronic toll collection has reduced dependence on cash at toll plazas. The rise in UPI payments also indicates the gradual expansion of digital payment options for highway users.

briefs.headline: Listing will change Tata way, put profit above philanthropy: Noel
briefs.deck: Noel Tata has expressed strong opposition to the potential listing of Tata Sons on public markets. He believes such a move may compromise the group's long-standing commitment to philanthropy over profit. Some trustees argue that listing could enhance governance and transparency while supporting charitable aims. The debate reflects differing views on the future ownership structure of the Tata…
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI:Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata has sharpened his opposition to a potential listing of 
Tata Sons
, arguing that bringing in public shareholders could upend a century-old ownership structure in which philanthropy sits above profit.
"My worry is that listing, which is what some people are proposing, will change the Tata way. And one day, if we have 30,000, 40,000 shareholders, profit may take precedence over philanthropy. I think that would fundamentally change the Tata way of working."
Framing the issue as central to the group's identity, Tata added: "The whole essence of Tata Group today is that 66% of profits of Tata Sons are used for philanthropic causes. That is unique in the world."
"Charity precedes commerce. Charity owns commerce. It's not the other way around," he said at the HT Leadership Summit on Saturday
His remarks come as Tata Sons faces pressure to comply with the Reserve Bank of India's upper-layer non-banking financial company (UL-NBFC) regulations, which require the holding company to list. Tata Sons remains the only entity on the RBI's UL-NBFC list that has not complied with the framework.
While Tata has publicly opposed a listing, some Tata Trusts trustees have taken the opposite view. Trusts vice-chairmen Venu Srinivasan and Vijay Singh have argued listing and philanthropy can coexist, citing foundation-owned global companies such as Novo Nordisk and Hershey. They contend a listing would not dilute the Trusts' controlling stake and could strengthen governance, transparency and accountability while enhancing the dividend stream that funds charitable activities.
The differences underscore a rare public divergence within the Trusts. Noel succeeded Ratan Tata after his death in October 2024, and the debate has exposed fault lines over the future ownership structure of the $180-billion group.
"Dividends from some of our listed companies, which come through the channel, become tomorrow's hospitals, tomorrow's flood relief, tomorrow's education institutions, tomorrow's relief for people in crisis," Tata said. "This profit becomes, in a way, a public good. It repeats itself every year, year on year, by design."
Defending the existing structure, he said: "In this particular case, the owner cannot die. The owner cannot be bought. And the owner cannot retire. So there is a continuity in the Tata way."
Some trustees, however, maintain that Tata Sons shareholding is held by public charitable trusts and that trustees act only as custodians and fiduciaries, not owners.
Tata also argued that remaining private gives Tata Sons the flexibility to support group companies in times of need.
"The other thing that staying private does is Tata Sons remains the backstop for all or any Tata companies that ever gets into trouble. And that is an important glue which keeps the entire group together."
"The moment you have a separate set of investors in Tata Sons that requires funding, they're quite right to ask, why do we want to make investments here? You should only be making investments in what will deliver and allocating capital to the most profitable ventures. And therefore the nature of the group is going to change."
At the same time, a listing would open new funding avenues for Tata Sons, giving it direct access to public equity markets and a broader debt investor base, options that are largely unavailable in its current form, some Tata observers said.
"Why tinker with something that has delivered such value for 150 years? Why do we want to change that?" Tata asked. He said the Trusts would "play a constructive role with the regulators, with others, to try and find a solution which keeps the Tata way the way it is."
Tata also backed the group's strategic direction but appeared to question its execution, in remarks seen as a veiled critique of Tata Sons chairman N Chandrasekaran.
"The strategic direction, as I've said now twice or thrice, remains the same. Philanthropy on one hand, nation building on the other hand. This is independent of the leadership, of personalities. This is embedded in the DNA of the group," he said. "I have not asked or questioned the direction of what we've done. 
I question sometimes the delivery of what we're doing."
"The question is, do we have the discipline when we execute projects and not the direction? How will projects with a long gestation period succeed if we don't have discipline? And how will we allocate capital to those projects?"
"So very clearly, direction is fine, but we also need discipline of execution in these very large projects," he said.

briefs.headline: Indians ditch gold for gemstones as sales jump 40%; stones cost Rs 5 lakh
briefs.deck: The growing preference for premium coloured gemstones as against gold is also translating into higher prices. Paraiba tourmalines, among the rarest gemstones, sell for around Rs 5 lakh per carat in India. Demand for these stones is particularly strong among high-net-worth buyers in Mumbai, followed by customers in Delhi and South India.
briefs.bodyText:
Looking beyond gold and diamonds, affluent buyers are in the market for coloured gemstones which are becoming an important growth segment for India’s high-end jewellery market.
Sales have risen 40% during the festive season as wealthy buyers show greater interest in alternatives to conventional gold and diamond jewellery.
The shift is evident in the increasing share of studded jewellery in the sales of organised retailers.
Rare Paraiba tourmalines, emeralds and more
The demand ranges from rare Paraiba tourmalines priced at around Rs 5 lakh per carat to emeralds, spinels, tanzanites and aquamarines.
At Kalyan Jewellers, such jewellery contributed slightly less than one-third of sales in the second quarter of FY27, which recently concluded, reflecting stronger demand for pieces featuring diamonds and coloured gemstones.
“Gemstones are moving from the margins to the centre of the jewellery conversation, and we are seeing this reflected in our numbers, with studded jewellery contributing 31% of our sales in the recently concluded quarter,” Ramesh Kalyanaraman, executive director, Kalyan Jewellers told ET.
Jewellers say these stones are attracting customers seeking exclusivity, distinctive designs and a more individual expression of luxury, while also looking for pieces they consider worthy of investment.
Kalyan Jewellers has identified two emerging patterns in consumer preferences.
In one, coloured gemstones are paired with natural diamonds as accent stones. In the other, the coloured gemstone takes centre stage in the jewellery design.
While the first approach has found wider acceptance across Indian markets, the second remains a niche segment that is gradually expanding, drawing buyers who want jewellery that reflects their individual tastes and stands apart through its design.
Kalyanaraman said demand for the second category, where coloured gemstones take centre stage in jewellery designs, is especially noticeable in Delhi, Jaipur, Surat, Ahmedabad, Bengaluru and Hyderabad.
Higher prices for gemstones
The growing preference for premium coloured gemstones is also translating into higher prices.
Paraiba tourmalines, among the rarest gemstones, sell for around Rs 5 lakh per carat in India. Demand for these stones is particularly strong among high-net-worth buyers in Mumbai, followed by customers in Delhi and South India.
Prices of certain rubies, emeralds and sapphires have climbed three to four times in the past two years.
Alok Sonkhiya, director of Valentine Group and former president of the Jewellers Association of Jaipur, said the increase has been driven by constrained mining supplies, rising interest from international collectors and a stronger preference for natural stones that have not undergone treatment. Jaipur is a major centre for cutting and polishing coloured gemstones.
“This festive season, coloured gemstones have done very well, and sales have surged by 40%,” he told the financia daily.
High-quality sapphires that have not been heat-treated have recorded annual price increases of 15-20%. Meanwhile, rare Kashmir and Burmese stones continue to fetch record prices at international auctions. Scarce varieties, including Paraiba tourmalines and spinels, are also witnessing significant appreciation.
Buyers increasingly seek distinctive jewellery
The changing profile of buyers is expanding the market beyond conventional bridal jewellery. Affluent women, high-net-worth individuals (HNIs) and CXOs are increasingly purchasing coloured gemstones for festive wear, gifts and personal collections. Younger consumers with higher incomes are also gravitating towards stones that offer exclusivity and make a distinctive design statement.
“Gold and diamonds have traditionally represented value and permanence, but coloured gemstones bring a different dimension to fine jewellery, one that is deeply personal. No two gemstones are quite alike, and it is this individuality of colour, character and natural formation that makes them so fascinating,” said Siddhartha Sacheti, creative director and CEO of Jaipur Gems.
Apart from emeralds and rubies, the company is witnessing greater interest in spinels, tourmalines, tanzanites and sapphires in a broad range of colours, he said.
The stronger demand is also evident in the amount consumers are willing to spend on these pieces. “Demand starts from 7 lakh onwards. Accessible prêt pieces such as rings and bracelets are driving festive gifting, while bespoke high-jewellery pieces command multi-crore valuations for rare, collector-grade stones,” said Renu Oberoi, founder and creative director of Renu Oberoi, a fine and luxury jewellery brand based in Mumbai’s Nariman Point.

briefs.headline: Sold commercial units & bought 2 flats, taxman denies Rs 2.5 crore relief on one - what ITAT said
briefs.deck: A man sold six commercial units in Mumbai and the sales generated long-term capital gains of around Rs 5 crore. He claimed a deduction of the same amount under Section 54F after investing in residential property. For this purpose, he purchased two flats in Wing A of a building but on separate floors. Agreements for both flats were executed and registered on the same date.
briefs.bodyText:
A taxpayer sells commercial properties and invests the proceeds in two residential flats. But the flats are on different floors. Does that automatically mean he can claim capital gains tax relief on only one of them?
In one such case, a taxpayer faced disallowance on capital gains exemption for the second flat. Read on to know why the Income Tax Appelate Tribunal (ITAT) Mumbai ruled in his favour:
What the case is about
A man sold six commercial units in Mumbai and the sales generated long-term capital gains of around Rs 5 crore. He claimed a deduction of the same amount under Section 54F after investing in residential property.
For this purpose, he purchased two flats in Wing A of a building but on separate floors. Agreements for both flats were executed and registered on the same date.
The Assessing Officer accepted the claim for one flat but rejected the deduction relating to the second, taking the view that Section 54F allowed relief for only one residential house. This resulted in a disallowance of Rs 2,51,31,621. The Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), National Faceless Appeal Centre, upheld the decision.
The appellate authority pointed to the fact that the flats were on different floors, had separate entrances and attracted stamp duty separately. In its view, the common building and lift did not change the fact that they were two distinct properties.
The man subsequently challenged this interpretation before ITAT. 
His counsel argued that both flats had been acquired together to accommodate the family as one residential unit.
His counsel submitted that adjacent flats that could be interconnected were not available, given the constraints of finding suitable residential accommodation in Mumbai. The two flats were in the same wing and accessible through a common lift, which the taxpayer relied on to support his argument that they were intended to function as one family residence.
Why ITAT ruled in favour of taxpayer
The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), Mumbai, ruled in favour of the taxpayer. The tribunal held that separate entrances, floors and registration documents did not, by themselves, prevent the two flats from qualifying as one residential house under Section 54F of the Income Tax Act.
The tribunal considered earlier judicial decisions, including the Delhi High Court's ruling in 
CIT v. Gita Duggal
 and the decision in 
Principal Commissioner of Income Tax v. Lata Goel
. These decisions supported the principle that residential accommodation need not always be confined to a single physical unit to qualify for the relevant capital gains relief.
The tribunal explained the test it applied: “What is relevant is the substance and functional character of the residential accommodation and whether the units, in the facts of the case, constitute one residential house.”
This meant that the question could not be settled merely by counting the number of registered units. The tribunal considered the circumstances in which the man had purchased the flats: both were acquired on the same date, from the same developer, in the same building and wing, and had identical areas and purchase prices. Their location on different floors was the principal distinguishing feature.
The fact that adjacent flats were said to be unavailable also helped explain the man’s decision to purchase units on different floors.
The tribunal held that the separate entrances and separate stamp duty payments did not, on their own, establish that the units had to be treated as two independent residential houses for Section 54F.
It observed: “The statutory provision does not prescribe that a residential house must necessarily be evidenced by a single registered instrument or must comprise one undivided physical unit.”
The judges drew a distinction between the physical layout of a property and its character as residential accommodation. A building may contain separate units that can be used independently, but that fact alone does not necessarily prevent the accommodation from being treated as one residential house for the purpose of the deduction.
Applying the principle to this case, the tribunal concluded: “We, therefore, find that the facts of the present case, considered in the light of the ratio laid down by the Hon'ble Delhi High Court in Gita Duggal (supra) and Lata Goel (supra), justify treating the two residential flats as constituting one residential house for the purposes of section 54F.”
The tribunal therefore found the disallowance relating to the second flat unsustainable. It directed: “We, therefore, set aside the order of the learned CIT(A) and direct the Assessing Officer to allow the deduction under section 54F in accordance with law.”

briefs.headline: TRAI crackdown on spam: Over 1.24 lakh mobile connections barred or disconnected in July-September
briefs.deck: A total of 1,10,325 telecom resources, including mobile numbers, were barred from outgoing services for 15 days for the first violation
briefs.bodyText:
Regulator Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) took enforcement action against more than 1.24 lakh telecom resources and blacklisted 374 entities for one year for violating unsolicited commercial communication (UCC) norms during July-September, as it stepped up efforts to curb spam calls and messages.
A total of 1,10,325 telecom resources, including mobile numbers, were barred from outgoing services for 15 days for the first violation, while 13,777 were disconnected for one year for repeat violations, according to TRAI's quarterly report for the second quarter of 2026-27.
The regulator also blocked 3,725 SMS headers and blacklisted 374 senders for one year, during which they cannot obtain fresh telecom resources.
TRAI received 15.29 lakh complaints of unsolicited commercial communications during the quarter, of which 7.23 lakh were classified as actionable. The complaints were registered against a backdrop of 714.01 billion calls and 702.28 billion SMSes originating from telecom networks across the country. “The complaint rate worked out to about 2.14 per million outgoing calls,” the report said.
The TRAI DND App remained the primary channel for reporting spam, accounting for 14.21 lakh, or 92.9%, of all complaints received during the quarter. The app had recorded 42.36 lakh downloads by September 30.
The regulator said Artificial Intelligence-based systems deployed by telecom operators flagged 19.9 billion incoming calls and SMSes as suspected spam during the quarter. These included 18.28 billion calls and 1.62 billion SMSes.
Telecom operators also issued more than 45.9 lakh warning notifications to entities suspected of sending spam communications. They conducted electronic know-your-customer (e-KYC) verification of 34,025 suspected senders, while 9,977 were disconnected for failing KYC verification.
TRAI has introduced dedicated numbering series to help consumers distinguish promotional calls from service and transactional communications.
Promotional calls are routed through the 140 series, while the 1600 series is designated for service and transactional calls by entities in banking, financial services and insurance, as well as government-to-citizen communications. A separate 1601 series was introduced on August 10 for service and transactional calls from utilities, logistics and delivery companies.
During the quarter, 15.27 billion promotional calls originated through the 140 series, of which 1.70 billion were blocked after verification against registered Do Not Disturb preferences. Registered telemarketers also originated 660.71 billion commercial SMSes, while 11.09 billion promotional messages were blocked after preference verification.
The report showed that 22.449 crore consumers had registered their preferences on the DND registry as of September 30, representing 16.64% of the country's 134.9-crore subscriber base. More than 112 crore subscribers had not registered any preference and remained accessible to commercial communications from registered senders and telemarketers.
TRAI said consumer awareness initiatives during the quarter included campaigns across radio, television, newspapers and social media, as well as 322 physical consumer awareness programmes involving around 31,000 participants. More than three billion SMSes were also sent to consumers to promote the DND App.
The regulator compiles the quarterly enforcement data on the basis of information furnished by telecom service providers.

briefs.headline: Apparel exports surge 20% in October on currency depreciation, but volume growth remains subdued
briefs.bodyText:
India’s apparel exports registered a 20.33% year-on-year growth (YoY) in dollar terms in October 2026, largely aided by the depreciation of the rupee, even as growth in the volume of garments shipped remained subdued.
Exporters said orders were strong across geographies, with demand providing an encouraging outlook for the sector. “If companies had not invested in expansion projects in the last one year, they would be running at full capacity now,” said a leading Coimbatore-based garment exporter. However, he cautioned that the increase in export value was unlikely to have been matched by a significant rise in shipment volumes.
A. Sakthivel, chairman of the Apparel Export Promotion Council (AEPC), said ready-made garment (RMG) exports recorded an encouraging growth of 20% in October compared with the corresponding month last year. In rupee terms, the growth was 30%.
“This positive performance signals a gradual recovery in the apparel export sector and reflects the improving demand for Indian garments in international markets,” he said.
AEPC data show that garment exports stood at $1.2 billion in October and $8.5 billion during April-October. YoY growth in September was 13.7%.
The U.S., the UK and the UAE remained the major export destinations. However, shipments to India’s free trade agreement partner countries declined between April and August, except for Oman.

briefs.headline: LPG distributors seek higher commissions, flexibility on new connections amid PNG push
briefs.bodyText:
LPG distributors have sought a revision in commissions, permission to issue fresh connections and a balanced approach to piped natural gas (PNG) expansion during an interaction with Union Petroleum Minister Hardeep Singh Puri on Friday.
Two industry executives who attended the meeting told The Hindu that distributors flagged rising operational costs amid declining refill sales as PNG gains ground.
“Our federation was encouraged by [Union Petroleum] Minister who heard our concerns at length. We told him that technological interventions as delivery authentication code (DAC) and e-KYC have made the overall mechanism cleaner,” an attendee said.
They said refill sales had suffered amid the PNG push, while commissions, last revised in October 2023, remained unchanged despite rising technology and safety costs.
“However, what has also happened is that refill sales have suffered amidst the PNG push and as a result, with [distributor] commissions not revised, our operational margins, be it for the requisite technology and safety have gone up,” they said.
Distributors also sought a “balancing act” between PNG and LPG, arguing that consumers should retain the freedom to choose. They urged the Ministry to allow fresh LPG connections, particularly in areas yet to be reached by PNG.
The Hindu has sought the government’s response.

briefs.headline: Iron ore capacity under-utilisation in major-producing states prompt concerns as India sets 2047 target
briefs.deck: The underutilised capacity is particularly significant as it largely involves hematite, the highest-grade variety of iron ore.
briefs.bodyText:
With India’s iron ore demand projected to rise to 772 million tonnes (MT) by 2047, miners in Odisha, the country’s largest iron ore reserve holder, are yet to utilise nearly 40% of their existing capacities, raising concerns over resource wastage and potential revenue losses.
The issue has come under judicial scrutiny, with both the Supreme Court earlier this month and the Odisha High Court in January flagging the underutilisation of mining capacities.
The Odisha High Court, while agreeing with petitioners who highlighted the sluggish operationalisation of mines despite environmental clearances, observed that the delay had resulted in an average annual revenue loss of ₹4,000 crore to the State.
However, industry sources, speaking on condition of anonymity, attributed the delays primarily to prolonged forest clearance procedures, which often exceed the stipulated 18-month timeframe.
Odisha’s iron ore conundrum
Data cited by petitioner Citizens’ Action Forum (Bhubaneswar) show that of the 246 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) of mining capacity granted environmental clearance in FY25, only around 159 MTPA had been operationalised.
Separately, data published by mining consultancy BigMint in June 2026 show that Odisha produced 158 MT of iron ore in FY26 against an environmentally cleared capacity of 278 MTPA, indicating capacity utilisation of nearly 60%.
The underutilised capacity is particularly significant as it largely involves hematite, the highest-grade variety of iron ore.
The shortfall also raises questions over India’s continued dependence on imports. According to the Mines Ministry, the country imported 12.3 MT of iron ore in FY26, incurring an expenditure of ₹11,115 crore.
Odisha accounted for more than 50% of India’s domestic iron ore production during FY26. Chhattisgarh contributed around 17.1%, followed by Karnataka at 16.6%. Capacity utilisation in the two states – albeit with significantly lower volumes than Odisha – stood at 62% and 80%, respectively, according to calculations based on BigMint data.
What courts said
In January, the Odisha High Court directed that mining rights be mandatorily transferred to state-owned National Mineral Development Corporation (NMDC) to ensure “optimum utilisation of the mines” and “eradicate any burden on the government exchequer”.
However, in its November 4 order, the Supreme Court concurred with the need for optimum utilisation of mineral resources but left the decision on transferring mining rights to the State government’s discretion, rather than making it mandatory.

briefs.headline: Why to tinker with something that has delivered value for 150 years: Noel Tata
briefs.deck: The trusts will work with regulators to find a solution to keep the Tata way as it is
briefs.bodyText:
Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata has cautioned that listing Tata Sons could fundamentally alter the group’s distinctive operating philosophy, with shareholder interests potentially taking precedence over philanthropy.
Amid growing demands for listing Tata Sons in line with the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) requirements, Mr Tata on Saturday made a strong pitch for maintaining the status quo.
“Why tinker with something that has delivered value for 150 years. Why do you want to change that,” he asked, referring to calls for listing from some Tata Sons board members and a section of Tata Trusts trustees.
He said the Trusts would engage constructively with regulators and other stakeholders to find a solution that preserves the group’s traditional governance structure.
“My worry is that listing, which is what some people are proposing, will change the Tata way. And one day, if we have 30,000-40,000 shareholders, profit may take precedence over philanthropy. And I think that will fundamentally change the Tata way of working,” he said at a function in New Delhi.
Explaining the philosophy, Mr. Tata said: “Charity precedes commerce. Charity owns commerce and it is not the other way around.”
He added that the group’s ownership structure ensured continuity. “The owner cannot die, the owner cannot be bought and the owner cannot retire. So there is continuity in what happens in the Tata way,” he said.
On the group’s strategic direction, Mr. Tata said its twin objectives of philanthropy and nation-building remained unchanged, but called for greater discipline in executing large projects involving long gestation periods and substantial capital commitments.
“Philanthropy on one hand. Nation building on the other hand. This is independent of leadership and personalities and this will continue. I do not question the direction of what we have done. I question, sometimes, the delivery of what we are doing,” he said.
“The question is, do we have the discipline when we execute projects, and not the direction? How will projects with a long gestation period succeed if we don’t have discipline? And how will we allocate capital to those projects?” he asked.
Recalling the legacy of Sir Ratan Tata and Sir Dorabji Tata, who dedicated their wealth to charity rather than passing it on to their families, he said their commitment to institution-building and helping the needy remained his guiding principle.
“This is the guiding light for me,” he said.

stories.headline: Aryna Sabalenka apologizes for on-court outburst in WTA Finals loss to Svitolina
stories.deck: The former top-ranked player from Belarus said on Saturday (November 14, 2026) she was upset by the behaviour of spectators during the match
stories.bodyText:
Aryna Sabalenka has apologized for an on-court outburst in her three-set loss to Elina Svitolina at the WTA Finals.
Video circulating widely on social media appeared to show Sabalenka swearing in a tirade during Friday's (November 13, 2026) 6-3, 3-6, 6-1 loss at the season-ending championships in Indian Wells.
The former top-ranked player from Belarus said on Saturday (November 14, 2026) she was upset by the behaviour of spectators during the match.
“My comment was not directed at Elina. I was frustrated with a small group of spectators who were aggressively cheering my mistakes, and I reacted emotionally in the moment,” Sabalenka posted on Instagram without mentioning what she said.
"That said, I should have handled my frustration differently and I apologize to anyone I offended. Elina played a great match, and I wish her all the best for the rest of the tournament.”
Sabalenka was visibly annoyed during the match, and she declined to speak with media afterward.
“There's many flags and many Ukrainian supporters are here and of course they want me to win in this particular match,” Svitolina said when asked about Sabalenka's online post.
“I have seen the glimpse of it because obviously it's in the social media, but yeah, I just hope the matches between us are respected. Sometimes in some matches there are not great comments towards me in regards of the war. It is like this in the social media sometimes that things are turned around a little bit,” she said.
Svitolina and others from her country have refused to shake hands with players from Russia and Belarus since Moscow's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 in line with policy set by the Ukrainian Tennis Federation.
Svitolina is set to play Russian teenager Mirra Andreeva in Sunday's final of the $10 million event.
Teen sensation Mirra Andreeva to face Svitolina
It’ll be rising teenager Mirra Andreeva against veteran Elina Svitolina in the WTA Finals title match, with Andreeva making her first appearance and Svitolina her third overall after a gap of seven years.
Andreeva is the first teen since 2004 to compete for the title after defeating American Jessica Pegula 6-3, 6-4 in the semifinals on Saturday. The 19-year-old Russian is having quite a year, winning her first Grand Slam title at the French Open and rising to No. 2 in the world.
Svitolina, a 32-year-old Ukrainian, raced past Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova 6-2, 6-1 in her 65-minute semi. Andreeva has a 2-1 career record against Svitolina.
Andreeva has yet to drop a set at the $10 million, season-ending event. Over four matches, she’s won 48 games and lost 18 — the fewest dropped in making the final since the round-robin format began in 2003.
“Super happy with how I have playing here so far,” she said. “Of course, the job is not done yet.”
Andreeva improved to 4-5 against Top 10 players this year, including wins over No. 2 Aryna Sabalenka, No. 6 Svitolina and No. 5 Pegula in the Southern California desert. She beat Svitolina 6-4, 6-0 in round-robin play earlier in the week.
Svitolina is the oldest player to reach the Finals title match since 37-year-old Venus Williams in 2017. She last made the Finals in 2018 and 2019, winning once and losing once.
“It’s incredible to think it’s been that many years and so many things happen in my life after the pregnancy, injuries and surgery,” said Svitolina, who became a mother four years ago. “I always wanted to be back in top 10 and play great game, and here I am. Very proud of the effort.”
Svitolina never let Noskova get going, with the Czech player done in by 27 unforced errors and 11 double faults.
“It was one of those where you feel like you don’t really belong on court, or you feel like you can’t do anything, nothing really works,” Noskova said. “Unlucky that it was in this competition at such a round, but it happens.”
Pegula broke Andreeva to take a 3-1 lead in the second set, but dropped five of the final six games to end her fifth consecutive Finals appearance. She lost in the 2023 final and was a losing semifinalist last year.
It was the first career meeting between Andreeva and Pegula, who was caught on a hot mic during a practice session at Indian Wells Tennis Garden referring to the teenager as a “diva” who “needs to be humbled.”
“The storyline writes itself,” Pegula said before the match. “I guess we had to play each other.”
Pegula said she later apologized to Andreeva.
“I think we’ve all seen that Mirra has a pretty good sense of humor with everything,” Pegula said. “She said she embraces it, so it was kind of funny. I was like maybe I need a little bit more of that in myself on the court. We’re all good.”
Pegula was coming off a career-high 16 aces in her final round-robin match. She had none Saturday and committed 31 unforced errors.
Andreeva had six double faults, but hit 58% of her first serves and also converted four of nine break points.
“I think she’s just very smart. Sees the court very well, moves well, anticipates well,” Pegula said. “She has a sneaky good serve. I think that’s something that’s a little underrated in her game.”
Andreeva ensured she’ll clinch a career-high ranking with the win, keeping Pegula from doing so.
“It’s not far from being No. 3 in the world,” Andreeva said, “so I don’t know if a lot changes with how I feel inside, but yeah, of course it’s a nice milestone.”
Fellow Russian Maria Sharapova was 17 when she reached the championship match of the 2004 Finals and beat Serena Williams in three sets.

stories.headline: Total Chess: Praggnanandhaa blunders, out of title race; Erigaisi keeps hopes alive
stories.deck: Only the top four players from each group will advance to knockout 1 and will fight for the title, while the rest will compete in the classification brackets
stories.bodyText:
Indian Grandmaster R Praggnanandhaa suffered a shock defeat after committing an inexplicable blunder from a winning position against Richard Rapport on day four of the Fast Classical competition at the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot in Budapest.
The 21-year-old made a late mistake in their first game and was immediately checkmated by Rapport.
As soon as Praggnanandhaa realised his mistake, he put his hand to his forehead, wearing a wry smile in disbelief.
“I don’t think I can play anything worse than that, so it’s fine!” Praggnanandhaa said.
The two drew their return encounter, leaving Praggnanandhaa at the bottom of Group B and it also ended his hopes of qualifying for the title knockouts.
His sister R Vaishali also bowed out of title contention after losing both her games to American GM Wesley So.
The Indian GM has four points from eight games, having lost six matches, won one and drawn one.
Only the top four players from each group will advance to knockout 1 and will fight for the title, while the rest will compete in the classification brackets.
However, Arjun Erigaisi remained in contention after ending Maxime Vachier-Lagrave's unbeaten Fast Classical run.
“It wasn't an easy game but I'm happy to win. I think in general Maxime is very quick under the clock, I'm happy I was able to put pressure on him,” Erigaisi said.
Following a draw in their first game, Erigaisi won the return with White in an endgame to join Vachier-Lagrave on 13 points.
Hans Niemann also moved to 13 points after a win and a draw against Bibisara Assaubayeva.
Niemann won the first game with White, but Bibisara held him to a draw in the day's longest game.
World No. 1 Magnus Carlsen drew both games against Shakhriyar Mamedyarov. Without a win in the group stage, the Norwegian was also eliminated from title contention.
Anish Giri took the outright lead in Group C with a win and a draw against Abhimanyu Mishra. Giri won an endgame with White in their first encounter.
Alireza Firouzja leads Group A on 13 points, while Fabiano Caruana holds a four-point advantage in Group B with 16 points. Dutch GM Anish Giri heads Group C on 13.
Jorden van Foreest joined Duda on 11 after exchanging wins with Andrew Hong.
Hong struck first with Black, but Van Foreest hit back with a win with Black in the return game. The three points apiece leave Hong on nine.
Levon Aronian and Nodirbek Abdusattorov also drew twice. Aronian reached nine points, level with Hong, while Abdusattorov has seven.
Firouzja thus carries a two-point lead into the final pair of group games.
Caruana and Liem Le drew both games, keeping the gap between Group B’s top two at four points. Caruana has 16 from four wins and four draws, while Le remains unbeaten on 12.
Two games remain for each player in the Fast Classic round-robin stage before the final standings determine places in the six knockout brackets.

stories.headline: Ronaldo tribute: All players wear No. 7, jersey immortalised with permanent change
stories.deck: Supporters in the stands displayed a banner reading "Obrigado, capi7ão" — "Thank you, captain" — alongside images of Ronaldo lifting the European Championship and Nations League trophies.
stories.bodyText:
Portugal paid tribute to 
Cristiano Ronaldo
 in their first match since the forward announced his retirement from international football, with every player wearing his iconic No. 7 jersey before their UEFA Nations League clash against Denmark on Saturday.
The tribute extended beyond the players, with the young mascots accompanying them also wearing the No. 7 shirt. Supporters in the stands displayed a banner reading "Obrigado, capi7ão" — "Thank you, captain" — alongside images of Ronaldo lifting the European Championship and Nations League trophies.
Portugal also made a change to the way the No. 7 is written on their shirts to honour Ronaldo's legacy. The new design features a horizontal line crossing through the number, similar to the way Ronaldo used to write it.
“Time to debut a new 7. Because there's one that will be eternal,” the Portuguese national team wrote on social media on Saturday. The post also included a goat emoji, referring to Ronaldo as the Greatest Of All Time.
The change ensures that Ronaldo's version of the No. 7 remains distinct from those who wear the number in the future. The forward made the number his identity during his career, becoming known as 'CR7'.
Ronaldo announced his international retirement on November 5, bringing an end to a career with Portugal that spanned 23 years. 
He made 246 appearances for his country and scored 146 goals, becoming the men's all-time leading international goalscorer.
He captained Portugal to their first major international trophy at Euro 2016 and also helped them win the Nations League in 2019 and 2025. His international career included appearances at six FIFA World Cups.
The tribute came nine days after his retirement announcement. Ronaldo's last appearance for Portugal was on September 24, in a 1-0 home win over Wales in the Nations League.
However, the celebrations before the Denmark match were followed by a disappointing result for Portugal. Playing their first game without Ronaldo, they suffered a 4-1 home defeat, with Rasmus Hojlund scoring twice for Denmark.
In the other League A Group Four match, Norway beat Wales 3-1 in Oslo. Antonio Nusa and Andreas Schjelderup scored before Erling Haaland converted a late penalty to complete the win.
Despite the defeat, Portugal remain at the top of the group with 12 points, three ahead of Denmark. Norway are third with six points, while Wales are at the bottom with three.
One round of league-phase matches remains. Wales will host Portugal, while Denmark will take on Norway on Tuesday.

briefs.headline: Wales beat New Zealand for first time since 1953
briefs.deck: Scrum-half Tomos Williams scored one of five Welsh tries in a superb individual performance as the home side ended a 34-match losing run against the three-time Rugby World Cup winners
briefs.bodyText:
Wales edged New Zealand 35-28 in the Nations Championship in Cardiff on Saturday (November 14, 2026) to claim their first victory over the All Blacks since 1953.
Scrum-half Tomos Williams scored one of five Welsh tries in a superb individual performance as the home side ended a 34-match losing run against the three-time Rugby World Cup winners.
Wales's heroic defence held out the visitors in the final 25 minutes after the All Blacks had made it a seven-point game thanks to Peter Lakai's try.
The victory is even more remarkable with Welsh rugby in dire straights after a poor run of results since the 2023 World Cup and a long line of off-field issues overshadowing the sport in the country.
Coach Steve Tandy made five changes from last weekend's tight win over Japan including starting Adam Beard at lock alongside Dafydd Jenkins to improve success at lineout.
New Zealand coach Davie Rennie handed full-back Beauden Barrett the captaincy for the first time on his 149th Test appearance in eight alterations from last Saturday's win over Scotland.
After just seven minutes, the hosts raced to a surprise 14-0 lead thanks to Williams and hooker Dewi Lake with the scrum-half providing the assist for the front-rower.
By the half-hour mark, Wales had a 21-7 lead with prop Archie Griffin diving over as New Zealand scrum-half Cortez Ratima kept the visitors in the game.
The All Blacks underlined their quality by the break as No 8 Wallace Sititi and winger Fehi Fineanganofo scored to bring the sides level at 21 points apiece.
Wales began the second-half as they did the first, and Williams set up another try with a miss-three pass to find Eddie James in the corner before winger Louis Rees-Zammitt dotted down with half an hour to play.
Flanker Lakai's try and Richie Mo'unga's conversion set up a tense final few minutes in the Welsh capital.
New Zealand pressed on the Wales line, having a couple of tries denied by being held up before the hosts managed to grind out a victory in front a joy-filled home crowd.

briefs.headline: Paris Hotel Project: Ronaldo and Pestana plan €60 million hotel; sixth property expected in 2027
briefs.deck: Cristiano Ronaldo expanded his Pestana CR7 hotel empire with a planned €60 million project in Paris, which was expected to open in 2027. The 210-room property was set to become the partnership's sixth hotel. With five existing properties across Funchal, Lisbon, Madrid, New York and Marrakech, the expansion highlighted how Ronaldo had built an international hospitality business beyond his football…
briefs.bodyText:
Cristiano Ronaldo
's ambitions had stretched far beyond the football pitch, and his growing hotel business offered a clear example. While the Portuguese superstar continued his playing career, his Pestana CR7 brand had already established a presence in five major destinations. Its next expansion was planned for Paris, where a €60 million hotel project was expected to bring another high-profile property into the portfolio in 2027. The development also showed how Ronaldo had turned his global sporting fame into a long-term business venture, one that did not depend entirely on his performances or playing career.
Cristiano Ronaldo's Pestana CR7 hotel empire had reached five destinations
Ronaldo's hotel partnership with Portugal's Pestana Hotel Group began in 2015. The first Pestana CR7 property opened in Funchal, Madeira, in 2016, close to the footballer's hometown. A Lisbon hotel followed in the same year, giving the brand its first two locations.
The business later expanded beyond Portugal. Properties opened in Madrid and New York in 2021, followed by Marrakech in 2022. By 2026, the partnership had five operating hotels across four destinations: Funchal, Lisbon, Madrid, New York and Marrakech.
The venture was structured as a 50-50 partnership between Ronaldo and the Pestana Group. While the footballer brought his CR7 identity, public profile and investment to the project, Pestana handled the hotel operations and management.
That arrangement allowed Ronaldo to take part in the hospitality business without having to manage its daily operations himself. It also helped the brand reach travellers looking for modern city hotels with a strong sports and lifestyle identity.
Paris hotel project added a €60 million expansion to Ronaldo's portfolio
The planned Paris property represented the next major step for Pestana CR7. The hotel was expected to become the brand's sixth location when it opened in 2027.
The development was part of the Austerlitz A7/A8 project in the French capital, near Gare d'Austerlitz. It was designed as a four-star property with 210 rooms, making it the largest hotel in the CR7 collection by room capacity.
The €60 million project was also expected to feature a landscaped rooftop, a swimming pool and a bar open to the public. Its location in Paris offered the brand access to one of the world's most visited cities and a major international tourism market.
The expansion came as the Pestana CR7 partnership marked its 10th anniversary in 2026. What began with a single hotel in Madeira had developed into an international hospitality brand.
For Ronaldo, the Paris project added another long-term commercial venture to a portfolio that had grown well beyond football. Even as questions about the later stages of his playing career continued, his hotel business had already been building a presence that could continue independently of his time on the pitch.

Kristian Clarke to Shreyas Iyer, Honing in on the off stump, on a good length. Iyer stabs it down the deck.
Drinks Break! New Zealand's pacers are calling the shots at the moment with quality bowling. Once again, they have managed to expose India's vulnerability to pace and bounce. Fisher has bowled with great heat, and the others have backed it up by bowling tight spells as well. India could have found themselves in an even more disastrous position had either of the two dropped chances been converted. Boundaries have been few and far between, and the two batters have had their fair share of luck along the way. With India needing a substantial partnership to repair the damage, Axar Patel's promotion up the order gives him the perfect opportunity to build one alongside Shreyas Iyer. Kristian Clarke continues after the break.
Blair Tickner to Axar Patel, Heart-in-mouth moment for Axar Patel! Tickner switches to over the wicket and delivers it on a hard length, on middle. Axar leans back but cannot drop his hands in time. The ball is skied off the face of the blade but it clears the keeper and the slip fielder comfortably, before dropping wide of deep third. They cross.
Blair Tickner to Axar Patel, More effort behind this ball by Tickner, on a shortish length, angled in on middle. Axar drops it with soft hands in front of point.
Blair Tickner to Axar Patel, Into the deck again, around off. Axar presses up on his toes and taps it to cover.
Blair Tickner to Axar Patel, Switches to around the wicket for the left-hander. Slams it into the wicket, on off. Not all that wide, but Axar is able to play the cut. Hits it into the ground but can't get it past Michael Bracewell at backward point, who makes the stop low to his left.
Blair Tickner to Shreyas Iyer, Slanting back in at the hips. Iyer hangs back and nurdles it to the right of mid-wicket for a run.
Blair Tickner to Shreyas Iyer, Edgy! Begins on a length, angled in on middle. Iyer gets his hands out in front and tries to clip it away. The ball holds in the surface and pops up off a leading edge but drops safely on the off side.
Double change. Blair Tickner is introduced into the attack, and he replaces Matthew Fisher.
Kristian Clarke to Axar Patel, Attacks the stumps with a length ball. Axar defends it from the crease.
Kristian Clarke to Axar Patel, Wide. Clarke goes short again, but this is too high. Axar arches back and initially shapes up for the upper cut, but then bails out. Wide given for height.
Kristian Clarke to Shreyas Iyer, At 132 kph, dug into the surface, outside off. Iyer drags the pull down to deep square leg and gets to the other end.
Kristian Clarke to Axar Patel, The length is pulled back, on off. Patel rides the bounce and punches it to the left of extra cover for a single.
Kristian Clarke to Axar Patel, FOUR! Beautiful shot. Angled away from the left-hander, on a good length. Axar gets the width to free his arms and he drives it on the up well to the right of mid off for a boundary.
Kristian Clarke to Shreyas Iyer, On the shorter side, on off. Iyer stands tall on top of the bounce and punches it between cover and mid off for a single.
Kristian Clarke comes into the attack as the first bowling change. He replaces Jacob Duffy.
Kristian Clarke to Shreyas Iyer, Starts with a good-length ball, a bit of nip back into the right-hander. Shreyas stabs it down off the back foot.
Matthew Fisher to Axar Patel, FOUR! Not entirely convincing, but Axar will take it. This is banged in short, but the line is a little too straight, beside the right shoulder. Axar gets up on his toes and gets his hands high. He manages to tickle it down to deep fine leg for a four.
Matthew Fisher to Axar Patel, Bashes the hard length, on middle and leg. Axar rises with the bounce and fends it down.
Matthew Fisher to Shreyas Iyer, Dug in short, on middle. Iyer pulls it down to deep square leg for a single.
Matthew Fisher to Shreyas Iyer, Jagging back in off a good length, on middle. Iyer keeps it out from the crease.
Matthew Fisher to Shreyas Iyer, Wide! Sprayed down leg, fuller in length. Iyer misses out on the glance.
Matthew Fisher to Shreyas Iyer, FOUR! Uppishly played, but it is in the gap. Not all that full, on off. Iyer does not get to the pitch of the ball and pushes out in front of his body. Ends up slicing the drive off the outer half, but in the gap between backward point and cover-point. The 50 is up for India with this boundary.
Matthew Fisher to Axar Patel, Pushed across the off stump. Axar flashes at the ball. It flies down to deep third for a single.
Jacob Duffy to Shreyas Iyer, Seaming back in, on a length, on off. Iyer shapes up for the big booming drive but then adjusts to the seam movement and pats it down to cover.
Jacob Duffy to Shreyas Iyer, FOUR! Nicely controlled by the Indian captain. Bowled into the surface by Duffy, on off. He does not get it high enough to trouble the right-hander. Iyer hops and rolls his wrists over the ball to pull it past mid-wicket for a four.
Jacob Duffy to Axar Patel, RUN OUT CHANCE! Axar Patel was gone had the throw hit. Angled away, on a good length. Axar knocks it on the rise wide of mid off and sets off for a quick single. Axar has to run around Duffy, who has his back to him. He bumps a bit with the bowler and as a result, he slows down while running the single. Mitchell Santner has a shy at the bowling end but misses, allowing Axar to get home.
Jacob Duffy to Shreyas Iyer, DROPPED! Loose, very loose, by Shreyas Iyer, but he gets away with it. Wider on off, on a good length. Iyer does not move his feet at all and just throws his hands at the ball. The outside edge is found and it flies quickly to Finn Allen at a wide slip, who is slow to react and tries to take the catch over his right shoulder, but it bursts through his grasp and goes away. They cross.
Jacob Duffy to Shreyas Iyer, FOUR! Gloriously driven. Duffy looks to go full and get the ball to dart back in. Ends up overpitching and Iyer cashes in. He leans into the stroke and drives it well to the left of mid on for a four.
Jacob Duffy to Shreyas Iyer, In the air for a bit, but safe. Duffy lands it on a good length, on middle and leg. Iyer pushes out in front and chips it beside the strip on the leg side.
End of the first Powerplay, one that belonged entirely to New Zealand. The Kiwis can now have 4 fielders outside the 30-yard circle until the 40th over, but Mitchell Santner is likely to keep the attacking fields in place rather than spread things out just yet.
Matthew Fisher to Axar Patel, A maiden from Fisher! Bowling from a wider angle, he goes full and outside off. Axar Patel looks to drive it down the ground, but the ball comes off the inner half of the bat and goes flat to the left of the bowler. Fisher, with very little time to react in his follow-through, attempts to pluck it out of the air to his left, but the ball deflects away towards mid off. Hard to call a dropped chance, as these just stick or they just don't. India end their Powerplay at 37/3.
Matthew Fisher to Axar Patel, At 143 kph, short of a length, on the leg stump, Axar gets behind the line and knocks it down the pitch.
Matthew Fisher to Axar Patel, Rears up at an awkward height, short on off, Patel rides the bounce and fends it with soft hands to point.
Matthew Fisher to Axar Patel, In the channel, angled away on a short length. Axar offers no shot.

briefs.headline: Batters need to fire as India targets series win
briefs.deck: India seeks a decisive series win as batters face seemingly New Zealand conditions in the final ODI after a batting collapse in the fourth match
briefs.bodyText:
The Indian batters would be determined to put up a much improved performance against the seamless ball with the series at stake in the fifth and final ODI against New Zealand on Sunday (November 15, 2026).
India leads 2-1 despite its second-heaviest loss by runs in ODIs in the fourth ODI here on Friday (November 13, 2026).
The Indian batters came a cropper in seaming conditions with Matt Henry effectively sealing the game for his team in his opening over by striking thrice. India were bowled out for 89 in 26.4 overs while chasing 334.
India needs to get better on pace-friendly surfaces, as it could get similar conditions in the 2027 ODI World Cup in South Africa.
Considering the collective failure of the batting line-up, it would not be fair to single out an individual. Having said that, Rohit Sharma and Shreyas Iyer, who had a forgettable captaincy debut, are yet to make an impact.
While Henry squared Rohit up with a beauty, Sheyas was caught in the crease against a sharp incoming delivery on Friday.
For Rohit and Virat Kohli, the game presents a final opportunity to enthral the crowd on probably their last tour of New Zealand. Kohli, too, had no response to Henry’s magic in the last outing.
Stand-in captain Shreyas said conditions changed drastically in favour of the bowlers in the second innings.
New Zealand, on the other hand, finds itself in another must-win situation as it aims to level the series. Opener Tim Seifert may have resurrected his career with a fifty in the fourth ODI, while Young, who was dropped twice in the slip cordon, went on to make a fine hundred.
The Indian pacers will need to stop the openers from taking the game away from them in the first 10 overs. The Black Caps have not lost a bilateral ODI series at home in seven years.
Match starts at 7.30 a.m. IST.

briefs.headline: Total Chess: Martirosyan inflicts first loss on Carlsen
briefs.bodyText:
Magnus Carlsen suffered his first loss in the Total Chess World Championship Tour pilot as Haik Martirosyan beat the World No. 1 and took the outright Group C lead on the third day of the Fast Classic stage here on Friday.
The Armenian won with white before drawing their return encounter, leaving Carlsen winless after six games. Martirosyan had 10 points to Carlsen’s five.
R. Vaishali secured her first Fast Classic victory, recovering from a defeat against Bibisara Assaubayeva to win their second meeting with an attack. The split results left the Indian on four points and the Kazakh on eight in Group D.
Arjun Erigaisi overturned a difficult position to beat Wesley So with black before drawing the return match. His nine points put him level with Hans Niemann, three behind leader Maxime Vachier-Lagrave.
R. Praggnanandhaa drew both games against Vladislav Artemiev in Group B, their first encounter lasting 89 moves. The Indian had four points and Artemiev five.
Martirosyan’s attacking victory over Carlsen helped him move one point clear of Anish Giri, who followed a draw against Ian Nepomniachtchi with a win after a long battle.
Nepomniachtchi and Shakhriyar Mamedyarov had seven points each. Mamedyarov drew twice against Abhimanyu Mishra, who had five.
Vachier-Lagrave drew his game against Niemann before winning the return with white to reach 12 points. So had four.
Group B leader Fabiano Caruana beat Vincent Keymer with black and drew their second game. Unbeaten with four wins and two draws, he had 14 points, four clear of Liem Le, who drew twice against Richard Rapport. Keymer had four points and Rapport five.
In Group A, Andrew Hong handed Alireza Firouzja his first group-stage defeat before the leader won their return meeting. Firouzja retained top spot with 11 points. Hong had six.
Jan-Krzysztof Duda stayed second on nine after two draws against Levon Aronian, who had seven. Jorden van Foreest beat Nodirbek Abdusattorov and drew the return, taking them to eight and five respectively.
Games seven and eight follow, with each player having four group games remaining.
(The writer is in Budapest at the invitation of Total Chess).

briefs.headline: The many challenges in front of Indian archers
briefs.bodyText:
Competitions with Indian bows have embraced significant changes, including fixing the distance for the qualification round at 30m and making it mandatory for every archer to shoot six arrows instead of three in each of the 12 ends.
These changes were adopted to iron out logistical challenges of moving targets for 50m and 30m segments and making archers better prepared for a possible switch to recurve or compound division.
After introducing these changes at the National junior championships in Jaipur last month, the Archery Association of India (AAI) implemented these at the elite National event here on Saturday.
“Shifting targets for 50m and 30m segments was a big problem. Earlier, with one big target face, every time an arrow bounced or hung, we had to stop as all four archers shooting at it were affected. Now, with four smaller faces, even if someone has an issue, others don’t get affected,” said tournament director Rupesh Kar.
“Instead of three, they are shooting six arrows. This will make them keep track of time and help switching to recurve or compound.”
Among 236 archers, Gusehaj Singh Sandhu (686) and 13-year-old Pratibha Kandara (661) topped in men’s and women’s sections respectively under the new format.
P. Heroba Singh, competing with Indian bows for two decades, found the format challenging. “The equation changes with six arrows. One must be mentally prepared,” he said.
Manipur’s archer-turned-coach Gitanjali Devi said, “Two 30m segments are better as arrows reach targets with good force and accuracy. It’s ideal for beginners.”
Recurve coach Sonam Thapa underlined the affordability of Indian bows, made of bamboo and wood in Manipur. “Most archers come from middle-class or poor families. A bamboo bow, which costs ₹5000-6000 unlike imported ones, is good to develop basic technique,” he said.
Pointing out the flip-side, coach Jiwanjot Singh Teja said, “The bow is fragile and causes injury. The draw length is limited and the poundage changes due to weather.”
However, international compound archer Rajat Chauhan highlighted another advantage. “One has to adjust as Indian bows and arrows lose shape during rains. But it makes one flexible,” said Chauhan, stressing the equipment’s role in the Indian context.

briefs.headline: Mushtaq Ali Trophy: TN holds its nerve to pip Railways
briefs.deck: Shahrukh and Rajkumar’s fireworks help the Sai Kishore-led side overcome a mid-innings wobble; Gurjapneet does the job after Toufik and Zuber nearly pull off a comeback victory for the institutional team; Mayank’s five-for the standout performance in the group
briefs.bodyText:
Shahrukh Khan (46 n.o., 30b, 5x4, 2x6) rediscovered his characteristic finishing touch to help Tamil Nadu fashion a six-run victory over Railways in a Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy Group B encounter at the Daly College ground here on Saturday.
Having been sent in, Tamil Nadu posted 172 for seven, recovering from a mid-innings wobble through a late assault by Shahrukh and R. Rajkumar (31, 13b, 1x4, 3x6), the duo adding 55 runs off 33 balls for the fifth wicket.
Opener Amith Sathvik set the tone with an enterprising 38 off 28 balls, striking seven fours. He added 65 runs with B. Sachin (33) for the second wicket. But Railways fought back, with leg-spinner Pradhyumn Parikh (two for 29) leading a disciplined bowling effort.
At 83 for three in 11.3 overs, Tamil Nadu needed a pick-me-up. Shahrukh obliged. He cut and lofted inside-out for fours against spin, and pulled a short ball from pacer Atal Bihari Rai over deep squareleg for six. Facing the same bowler in the final over, he sat deep inside the crease to launch another six over cow corner before dispatching a full toss to deep midwicket for four.
Rajkumar, as is typical of him, took the spinners downtown, smoking a straight six each off Pradhyumn and left-arm tweaker Mohammad Saif.
Railways stumbled early in the chase. Slinger Athisayaraj Davidson (three for 47), who returned to Tamil Nadu’s T20 fold after eight years, made an immediate impression, removing both openers in his first over.
Railways slipped to 54 for four in the PowerPlay before Varun Chakaravarthy (two for 17), at his frugal best, struck twice off successive deliveries to leave it reeling at 69 for six. He bowled Saif and had Kritagya Singh edging one to Shahrukh at slip.
Toufik Mondal (57, 22b, 5x4, 5x6) and Zuber Ali (46), however, revived the contest with a 69-run seventh-wicket stand off just 31 balls. But Athisayaraj returned to break the partnership before Gurjapneet Singh held his nerve to defend 11 runs in the final over.
Group-B’s standout performance came in the last match of the day. Mayank Yadav, playing for Delhi for the first time since 2023, marked his return with a terrific three-over spell of five for 14 as Delhi thrashed Jammu & Kashmir by 103 runs at the Holkar Stadium.
